14	# The Long-Term Sequential Development Model
15	
16	**What it is** — A pyramid model for an athlete's career: a broad base of **multilateral development** (childhood) → increasing **specialized training** (junior years) → **high performance** (maturity). The proportion of sport-specific work rises as the athlete matures — very small during the multilateral phase, then growing; for advanced athletes, ~60–80% of training time is sport-specific, the rest developing biomotor abilities (the exact ratio varies by sport: ~90% specific in long-distance running, ~40% in high jump). Bompa gives per-sport guideline ages for *starting training*, *starting specialization*, and *reaching peak performance* (e.g. specialization generally not before ~14–15 in most sports; Russian longitudinal data suggested not before age 15).
17	
18	**Why it works** — Three longitudinal studies (East German 14-year, Russian survey, and a tennis study) found athletes with a strong multilateral base reached higher ultimate performance, with fewer overuse injuries and less burnout, than early specializers — who progressed faster initially but plateaued, lost confidence, and faced more pressure. The base builds the physiological and psychological capacity that specialization later draws on.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Designing youth/developmental pathways; resisting pressure to specialize a fast-developing young athlete too early; setting sport-appropriate specialization timing; setting the general→specific ratio by training age.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Some early-entry sports (women's gymnastics, figure skating, diving, swimming) legitimately require young specialization due to early peak ages — the model bends to the sport's maturation demands. The guideline ages are rough, not prescriptive per individual (use [[heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]]). Deepens [[principle--multilateral-before-specialization]].
23	
24	**Example** — A talented 12-year-old showing rapid sport-specific progress is deliberately kept on a broad multilateral program, with specialization phased in around 14–15, to protect the long-term performance ceiling rather than chase early wins.
25

# The Long-Term Sequential Development Model

**What it is** — A pyramid model for an athlete's career: a broad base of **multilateral development** (childhood) → increasing **specialized training** (junior years) → **high performance** (maturity). The proportion of sport-specific work rises as the athlete matures — very small during the multilateral phase, then growing; for advanced athletes, ~60–80% of training time is sport-specific, the rest developing biomotor abilities (the exact ratio varies by sport: ~90% specific in long-distance running, ~40% in high jump). Bompa gives per-sport guideline ages for *starting training*, *starting specialization*, and *reaching peak performance* (e.g. specialization generally not before ~14–15 in most sports; Russian longitudinal data suggested not before age 15).

**Why it works** — Three longitudinal studies (East German 14-year, Russian survey, and a tennis study) found athletes with a strong multilateral base reached higher ultimate performance, with fewer overuse injuries and less burnout, than early specializers — who progressed faster initially but plateaued, lost confidence, and faced more pressure. The base builds the physiological and psychological capacity that specialization later draws on.

**When to apply** — Designing youth/developmental pathways; resisting pressure to specialize a fast-developing young athlete too early; setting sport-appropriate specialization timing; setting the general→specific ratio by training age.

**When NOT to apply** — Some early-entry sports (women's gymnastics, figure skating, diving, swimming) legitimately require young specialization due to early peak ages — the model bends to the sport's maturation demands. The guideline ages are rough, not prescriptive per individual (use [[heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]]). Deepens [[principle--multilateral-before-specialization]].

**Example** — A talented 12-year-old showing rapid sport-specific progress is deliberately kept on a broad multilateral program, with specialization phased in around 14–15, to protect the long-term performance ceiling rather than chase early wins.

# Soviet Sport-School Guideline Ages by Sport (Start, Specialize, Peak)

**What it is** — A per-sport table (Table 1.2) of recommended ages to begin a sport,
begin specialization, and expect high performance, drawn from the Soviet sports-school
system. Examples: basketball 7-8 / 10-12 / 20-25; gymnastics (women) 4-5 / 10-11 / 14-18;
gymnastics (men) 5-6 / 12-14 / 18-24; swimming 3-7 / 10-12 / 16-18; track-and-field 6-7 /
13-14 / 18-23; weightlifting 10-11 / 17-18 / 21-28; wrestling 10-11 / 15-16 / 24-28 (17
sports listed in total). Early, intense specialization is explicitly discouraged in
strength and endurance sports for children; the average age of Soviet Olympians in the
era cited was about 24, with fewer than 10% under age 20. (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp.
24-25.)

**Why it works** — Same underlying rationale as this library's existing long-term
athletic development material: early specialization in strength/endurance sports produces
faster short-term progress but a lower ultimate ceiling and more attrition, because the
young athlete has not built the broad physical base specialization later draws on.

**When to apply** — As a more granular, sport-by-sport reference table alongside this
library's existing LTAD guidance. It converges with, and adds numeric detail beyond, the
Bompa library's
[[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model|Long-Term Sequential Development
Model]], which states a general "not before ~14-15" specialization guideline but does not
break it out by individual sport the way this table does.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a 20th-century Soviet sports-school table, not a modern,
population-representative dataset; individual biological maturation varies (see
[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age|Biological vs Training
Age]]), and American collegiate sport pathways (e.g. football) do not map cleanly onto
these Soviet age bands. Treat the specific ages as illustrative, not prescriptive, for a
Baylor Athletics context.

**Example** — The table's general caution against early strength/endurance specialization
supports keeping a young multi-sport athlete on broad physical preparation rather than
early single-sport strength specialization, consistent with existing LTAD guidance already
in this library.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]] (reciprocal link
recommended there: add a line noting Supertraining Table 1.2 gives per-sport numeric ages
that concretize this framework's general specialization-age guidance).

type: library-entry
kind: principle
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.4"
topic: specificity of training
category: [specificity, exercise-selection, programming]

# Strength Training Adapts Along (at Least) Ten Independent, Narrow Dimensions

**What it is** — Strength gains transfer narrowly, not generally, across at least ten
independent dimensions: type of muscle contraction, movement pattern, region/range of
movement, velocity of movement, force of contraction, muscle fibre recruitment,
metabolism, biochemical adaptation, flexibility, and fatigue. Training that improves one
dimension often produces little or no improvement on the others, even when the same
muscle groups are involved. Specificity is explicitly distinguished from simulation:
mimicking a sport movement with added resistance is not the same as training the specific
factors above, and can actually distort the neuromuscular programming needed for the real
skill because of changes in center of gravity, moment of inertia, and mechanical
stiffness introduced by the resistance. (PDF pp. 38-39, printed pp. 27-28.)

**Why it works** — Strength adaptation is produced and expressed by the nervous and
muscular systems together (see
[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]); the specific
demands (velocity, joint angle, contraction type, metabolic pathway) shape which
recruitment patterns, fibre types, and biochemical pathways are trained, so a change in
any one of those parameters can produce a materially different, largely non-transferable
adaptation. This is one of the more broadly replicated findings in strength and
conditioning research, independent of this text.

**When to apply** — As the master reasoning check before assuming an exercise "transfers"
to a sport skill: ask which of the ten dimensions the exercise actually matches (velocity,
region of movement, contraction type, etc.), not just whether it uses similar muscles.
Directly supports Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky, Ch4.3), already taught in HHPR
5355 and part of Eric's baseline, as the applied extension of this same specificity logic
to exercise selection.

**When NOT to apply** — Don't use "specificity" as an argument against any general
preparation work; the text elsewhere (1.1, and the department's own multilateral/LTAD
material) supports building a general base before narrowing to sport-specific work. This
principle governs which dimensions transfer, not whether general work has value at an
earlier training age.

**Example** — Heavy squat strength does not automatically transfer to high-velocity sprint
force production (different point on the velocity dimension) even though both use similar
musculature; each needs its own specific training exposure.

**Related** — [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]],
[[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]].

type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.4"
topic: velocity and contraction-mode specificity
category: [specificity, velocity, exercise-selection]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# High-Velocity Training Transfers to Low Velocity Better Than the Reverse; Contraction Modes Barely Cross Over

**What it is** — Two specific, cited findings under the specificity umbrella: (1)
low-velocity isokinetic training improves low-velocity strength but has minimal effect on
high-velocity strength; high-velocity isokinetic training improves high-velocity strength
and transfers somewhat better to low-velocity strength than the reverse direction
(Moffroid & Whipple 1970; Perrine & Edgerton 1981; Kanehisa & Miyashita 1983b). (2)
Contraction-mode adaptations are narrow: concentric-eccentric (weightlifting-style)
training raises competitive strength but produces only small isometric or concentric
isokinetic gains; isometric training raises isometric strength but not concentric
isokinetic strength; elbow-extension training with weights increases triceps strength and
girth without a matching isokinetic-strength change. Static and dynamic training even
produce different microscopic structural changes in the muscle. (PDF pp. 38-40, printed
pp. 27-29.)

**Why it works** — Force-velocity curve position (see
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]) and contraction-mode
recruitment patterns are trained narrowly because different neural drive strategies and
structural adaptations underlie each; high-velocity training likely also recruits fast-
twitch units that contribute somewhat at slower speeds, which is the proposed reason the
transfer is asymmetric rather than symmetric.

**When to apply** — When selecting exercise velocity and contraction mode, match both to
the sport action being targeted, and bias toward including higher-velocity work when in
doubt, since it transfers in both directions somewhat, whereas slow, heavy work transfers
poorly to fast actions. Use as a rationale for including isometric mid-thigh pull or
isometric testing/training (already part of Baylor's ForceDecks protocol) as its own
distinct quality, not a proxy for dynamic 1RM strength.

**When NOT to apply** — These are 1970s-1980s isokinetic-dynamometer studies; isokinetic
machine training is a narrow, lab-style modality rarely used in current collegiate S&C
practice, and this specific transfer asymmetry has not been independently re-verified here
for free-weight or plyometric training modes. Do not assume the same asymmetric-transfer
ratio applies to, say, barbell velocity-based training without separate evidence.

**Example** — An athlete tested for isometric mid-thigh pull strength should not be assumed
to have an equivalent dynamic 1RM or sprint force capability; each needs its own
assessment and, if targeted, its own specific training exposure.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]].

category: [specificity, testing, exercise-selection]

# The Bilateral Deficit: Two Limbs Together Produce Less Force Than the Sum of Each Alone

**What it is** — Force produced during a bilateral (two-limb, e.g. barbell) contraction is
usually less than the sum of the forces each limb produces individually (e.g. dumbbells),
a phenomenon called the bilateral deficit, accompanied by reduced integrated EMG
suggesting the prime movers are less activated bilaterally (Coyle et al. 1981;
Vandervoort et al. 1984). The deficit is reported as insignificant in athletes who always
use their limbs simultaneously in their sport (e.g. weightlifters), and the text
recommends athletes whose sport involves bilateral action of the same muscle groups train
bilaterally to minimize the deficit (Secher, 1975). (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28.)

**Why it works** — The deficit is attributed to a neural, not mechanical, limitation:
reduced activation of the prime movers during simultaneous bilateral effort, which
training the specific bilateral pattern appears to reduce over time — another instance of
narrow, mode-specific neuromuscular adaptation.

**When to apply** — When deciding whether to prioritize bilateral (back squat, bench,
clean) or unilateral (split squat, single-leg press, lunge) exercise variants: match the
training mode to how the sport actually loads the limbs. For sports with genuinely
unilateral force production (sprinting, most cutting and change-of-direction actions),
this argues for meaningful unilateral training exposure, not exclusively bilateral lifts,
since bilateral-only training may under-develop the single-limb activation football and
track actions actually require.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this to argue against bilateral lifts altogether;
compound bilateral lifts remain valuable for maximal strength and are appropriate where
the sport itself uses bilateral effort (e.g. some blocking or lifting actions). The
deficit's size and trainability likely vary by athlete and lift, and no specific
magnitude is given in this text for team-sport athletes.

**Example** — A sprinter's single-leg force production during ground contact is not fully
predicted by their bilateral back squat strength alone; programming that includes
single-leg strength work targets the bilateral deficit gap directly relevant to sprint and
change-of-direction performance.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]].

reduced activation of the prime movers during simultaneous bilateral effort, which

**When to apply** — When deciding whether to prioritize bilateral (back squat, bench,
clean) or unilateral (split squat, single-leg press, lunge) exercise variants: match the
training mode to how the sport actually loads the limbs. For sports with genuinely
unilateral force production (sprinting, most cutting and change-of-direction actions),
this argues for meaningful unilateral training exposure, not exclusively bilateral lifts,
since bilateral-only training may under-develop the single-limb activation football and
track actions actually require.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this to argue against bilateral lifts altogether;
compound bilateral lifts remain valuable for maximal strength and are appropriate where
the sport itself uses bilateral effort (e.g. some blocking or lifting actions). The
deficit's size and trainability likely vary by athlete and lift, and no specific
magnitude is given in this text for team-sport athletes.

**Example** — A sprinter's single-leg force production during ground contact is not fully
predicted by their bilateral back squat strength alone; programming that includes
single-leg strength work targets the bilateral deficit gap directly relevant to sprint and
change-of-direction performance.

# Types of Maximal Strength (CFmax, TFmax, Fmm, Relative Strength)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) separates "maximum strength" into a
ladder of distinct maxima, from lowest to highest: training maximum (TFmax, the training
1RM, the heaviest load one can lift without a large emotional/heart-rate spike),
competitive maximum (CFmax, the true 1RM produced under optimal competitive motivation),
and absolute strength (Fmm, "maximum of all maxima," the involuntary ceiling reachable
only under electrical stimulation or a sudden reflex-recruited load, e.g. a sudden drop
or stretch reflex). Relative strength is strength per unit bodymass for a given lift.
Voluntary maxima also rank by contraction type, in order of magnitude: eccentric >
isometric > concentric. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1-2.)

**Why it works** — Nervous system inhibition (protective feedback, comparable to a
mechanical governor) normally prevents a muscle from contracting to the point of
structural failure. Competitive arousal and motivation reduce that inhibition further
than routine training effort does, which is why CFmax exceeds TFmax; involuntary or
reflex-driven recruitment removes still more of it, which is why Fmm exceeds CFmax.

**When to apply** — Use this ladder to decide which maximum should anchor programmed
intensity. The text argues the competitive maximum, not the daily training maximum,
should set %-based intensity zones for higher-level athletes, because CFmax stays
comparatively stable while TFmax fluctuates day to day. For Baylor's own testing stack,
this maps onto why VBT-estimated 1RM (Perch) is preferred over live 1RM attempts:
estimating toward a target mean velocity approximates a stable maximum without forcing a
true CFmax-level competitive attempt in the weight room. See
`method-baseline.md` "Testing and assessment."

**When NOT to apply** — This is a terminology and reasoning framework, not a measured
protocol; none of the four maxima are routinely measured directly at Baylor (Fmm requires
electrical stimulation or reflex loading, which is impractical and carries injury risk).
Treat it as a mental model for why training-day and competition-day 1RMs diverge, not as
a set of numbers to test for. The eccentric > isometric > concentric ordering is a general
tendency, not a fixed ratio; it varies by joint angle, velocity, and muscle group (1.2).

**Example** — An athlete's best training-day squat (TFmax) is consistently lower than
what they hit in a max-out competition or meet (CFmax); programming off the meet number
rather than a re-tested gym max avoids under-loading the athlete for weeks after a strong
competitive performance.

**Related** — [[claim--voluntary-involuntary-strength-reserve-magnitudes]] (the numeric
gaps between these maxima); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
(a practical field proxy for the same voluntary/involuntary gap).

# The Voluntary-Involuntary Strength Reserve Has a Measured Size

**What it is** — Two cited figures quantify how much force voluntary effort leaves
unused relative to the athlete's true ceiling. (1) In experienced weightlifters, the mean
gap between training maximum (TFmax) and competitive maximum (CFmax) is about 12.5 ± 2.5%,
larger in heavier weight classes (Zatsiorsky, 1995; PDF p. 13, printed p. 2). (2) Under
involuntary or hypnotic conditions, strength output can rise by up to 35% in untrained
people, but by less than 10% in trained athletes (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2, no primary
citation given in text for this figure).

**Why it works** — Both numbers describe the same phenomenon from different angles: a
protective neural inhibition normally holds voluntary output below the muscle's true
contractile ceiling, and anything that reduces that inhibition (competitive arousal,
hypnosis, involuntary reflex recruitment) exposes more of it. Training narrows the
untapped reserve because part of the strength-training adaptation is learning to
recruit and inhibit less, not just growing tissue.

**When to apply** — As a coaching narrative for why max-effort numbers move around by
context (weigh-in day nerves, meet atmosphere, testing environment), and to set the
expectation that a smaller gap between training and competitive/testing efforts is
itself a marker of higher training status.

**When NOT to apply** — The hypnosis figure has no primary citation in the text and
should be treated as a single, unverified secondary claim, not a number to plan around.
The 12.5 ± 2.5% weightlifting figure is specific to experienced Olympic weightlifters
under meet conditions; it should not be assumed to transfer directly to team-sport
athletes tested on a force plate rather than in a weightlifting competition. Do not use
either number as a correction factor applied to Baylor's own 1RM or IMTP data without
independent verification.

**Example** — An athlete who tests near-identically on a submaximal VBT-estimated 1RM and
a rare true max attempt is showing a small reserve gap; a large, inconsistent gap between
estimated and tested max may point to arousal/readiness on test day rather than a change
in underlying capacity.

**Related** — [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]].

# Strength Increase Is Initiated by Neuromuscular Stimulation, Not Muscle Size

**What it is** — "The fundamental principle of strength training... is that all strength
increase is initiated by neuromuscular stimulation." Strength is framed as a function of
how powerfully and efficiently muscle is activated by the nervous system first, with
hypertrophy as a downstream, longer-term structural consequence of a given stimulus
regime, not the driver of early gains. (PDF pp. 17-18, printed pp. 6-7.)

**Why it works** — Hypertrophy is a slow structural adaptation; force output can rise
well before meaningful cross-sectional area change through improved recruitment,
firing rate, and coordination of the muscle already present. This is one of the more
independently replicated findings in strength physiology outside this text (early-phase
strength gains preceding measurable hypertrophy is a standard finding in resistance
training research), which is why this entry is rated `proven` rather than `supported`
despite the book being the citation vehicle here.

**When to apply** — Explains early-training-block strength gains in novice athletes that
outpace any visible muscle growth, and justifies technique/coordination-focused early
programming (see Tracy Fober's "chisel, not sledgehammer" standard in Eric's baseline)
before chasing load or hypertrophy. Also explains why detraining strength loss can
outpace measurable muscle loss: neural efficiency degrades faster than tissue.

**When NOT to apply** — This does not mean hypertrophy is unimportant for strength at
higher training ages; the text itself notes maximal strength "depends to a great extent"
on adequate muscle cross-section. Do not use this principle to justify skipping
hypertrophy-phase work for athletes past the early-adaptation window, where structural
gains matter more for continued strength progress.

**Example** — A freshman who has never lifted seriously often adds meaningful strength in
the first 4-6 weeks of a program with little visible size change; that gain is
predominantly neural (coordination, recruitment, reduced antagonist co-contraction), not
tissue growth.

**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] (the
mechanisms by which this happens).

# Functional vs. Structural Resistance Training

**What it is** — Two basic categories of resistance training effect: structural training
targets muscle hypertrophy (and some tissue flexibility); functional training targets
performance qualities (static strength, speed-strength, muscular endurance, reactive
ability) through four neural mechanisms: (1) intermuscular coordination — sequencing and
synchronizing action between different muscle groups; (2) intramuscular coordination —
control within one muscle via number encoding (how many fibres are recruited), rate
encoding (firing frequency), and pattern encoding (sequencing of fibre types); (3)
facilitatory/inhibitory reflex processes; (4) motor learning, programming the CNS to
execute a specific task. No training is purely structural; all training is functional to
some degree and may also elicit structural change. (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7.)

**Why it works** — Force output for a given movement is the product of both how much
contractile tissue exists (structural) and how effectively the nervous system recruits,
times, and sequences that tissue (functional). Early or stagnation-phase training gets
more return from the functional side because coordination has more room to improve;
structural change is slower and more load-dependent.

**When to apply** — Use as a diagnostic lens when an athlete's strength stalls: ask
whether the limiter is likely structural (needs more hypertrophy-phase volume) or
functional (needs improved coordination, rate coding, or motor learning of the specific
lift/skill). The text explicitly states functional stages should precede structural
stages both for beginners and during a plateau at an advanced level (see 1.2, Ch2).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual split, not a measured diagnostic; number,
rate, and pattern encoding are not directly observable from a force plate or barbell
velocity alone; inferring which mechanism is limiting a given athlete is coach judgment,
not a test result. Don't treat "functional training" here as synonymous with the modern
commercial-gym use of the term (balance boards, unstable surfaces); Verkhoshansky's
meaning is specifically about neural coordination and recruitment.

**Example** — A lifter whose 1RM is stagnant despite visible muscle gain may be limited by
intermuscular coordination (poor bracing/synchronization under heavy load) rather than by
insufficient muscle; technique and coordination work, not more volume, is the higher-value
fix.

**Related** — [[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]].

# Restrictive, Repetitive Patterns May Overspecialize the Nervous System

**What it is** — Drawing on neuroplasticity research (Rosenzweig, Diamond, Greenough,
cortical reorganization in amputees and stroke patients), the text argues the nervous
system rewires quickly (within minutes, not years) around whatever movement pattern is
repeated, and lists practical inferences: avoid machines that restrict joint movement to
one plane/pattern (they can reprogram the brain toward that restricted pattern and reduce
sport-specific capability); avoid over-reliance on ergogenic devices (lifting belts, wrist
wraps, shoe wedges) that can make efficient unassisted movement harder later; favor
planned variation of means, methods, and exercises over fixed repetition of the same
weights or machines; respect individual movement style rather than forcing one stereotyped
technique on every athlete. (PDF pp. 19-20, printed pp. 8-9.)

**Why it works** — The underlying neuroscience (adult cortical plasticity, rapid synaptic
change, constraint-induced reorganization in rehab patients) is well established. The
extension to healthy-athlete strength training — that machine use or ergogenic aids will
measurably "reprogram" sport-specific neural patterns — is the text's own inference, not a
finding directly tested in athletes in this section.

**When to apply** — As a rationale for favoring free-weight, multi-planar, compound
movement over single-joint machine work when the goal is direct transfer to a sport skill,
and for planning intentional exercise variation across a training block rather than
running the same fixed machine circuit indefinitely. This is broadly consistent with the
department's own basic-movement-before-machines philosophy in the HHPR baseline.

**When NOT to apply** — Treat as contested where it implies routine machine use or belts
during max lifts causes lasting neural harm to sport skill; there is no dose-response
evidence cited here, and machines and supportive equipment remain standard, safe tools in
most strength programs, including at Baylor, with no established injury or transfer cost
at typical use levels. Do not use this heuristic to argue against belts for heavy
compound lifts, where the safety benefit is well established elsewhere.

**Example** — Programming a hip-thrust machine as the sole posterior-chain exercise for a
sprinter, with no free-weight hip hinge or sprint-pattern work anywhere in the week, is the
scenario this heuristic warns against; it does not warn against occasional supported
machine use as part of a varied program.

**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]].

# Estimating Strength Deficit by Comparing a Static-Start Jump to a Dip/Countermovement Jump

**What it is** — Strength deficit is defined as the gap between an athlete's maximum
voluntary strength in a given action and their absolute strength (Fmm), the involuntary
ceiling for that same action (see [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]). True Fmm
requires electrical stimulation, which is impractical and risky to test directly. As a
field proxy, the text proposes comparing a vertical jump from a static, knees-flexed start
(no countermovement) against a vertical jump preceded by a sudden dip (a countermovement
that recruits the stretch reflex and involuntary/reactive contribution). A small
difference between the two jumps suggests the athlete is already recruiting most of their
available force voluntarily, i.e. training should emphasize raw force/strength capacity;
a large difference suggests a bigger untapped reactive/neural reserve, i.e. training
should emphasize "shock" and ballistic (reactive) methods instead. (PDF p. 20, printed
p. 9; the explosive-strength-deficit formalism, Fmax vs. Fmm, is credited to Zatsiorsky,
1995, discussed further via the force-time curve in Ch3.)

**Why it works** — A countermovement recruits the stretch-shortening cycle and a degree
of involuntary reflex potentiation that a static start cannot access; the size of the
resulting performance gap is a rough behavioral index of how much of the athlete's
reactive/neural potential is already expressed voluntarily versus still latent.

**When to apply** — This maps directly onto Baylor's existing ForceDecks battery: the
squat jump (quarter-squat start, static, no countermovement) versus the countermovement
jump (x3) that Applied Performance already runs. Comparing SJ height/output to CMJ
height/output for the same athlete is effectively running this framework's proposed
proxy with instrumented, repeatable data instead of a stopwatch-and-tape-measure
comparison. A small SJ-CMJ gap (or a low CMJ-to-SJ ratio) suggests programming should lean
toward raw strength/force development; a large gap suggests more reactive-strength/shock
method work (depth jumps, plyometrics) is likely to pay off, consistent with the reactive
strength/mRSI emphasis already in the department's daily monitoring.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a directional heuristic from a Soviet-era text, not a
validated cutoff; no threshold percentage is given for "small" versus "large" gap, and the
modern jump-testing literature uses more specific derived metrics (RSI, mRSI, eccentric
utilization ratio) that were developed independently of this framework and should be the
primary interpretive tool. Treat this entry as the conceptual ancestor of that later
metric family, not a replacement for it. Do not use a single SJ/CMJ comparison on one test
day to make a training-emphasis decision; use trended data.

**Example** — An athlete with SJ and CMJ heights within 1-2 cm of each other is a candidate
for a strength-emphasis block; an athlete with a large CMJ advantage over SJ (a high
eccentric utilization ratio) is more likely to respond to reactive/plyometric emphasis.

**Related** — [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]].

# Strength Deficit Size Points to a Different Training Method

**What it is** — If an athlete's strength deficit (see
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]) is large for a given muscle
group, the text recommends near-maximal neuromuscular stimulation (weightlifting or
plyometric methods) or, if very large, Compensatory Activation Training (CAT) with 5-8RM
loads. If the deficit is small, it recommends submaximal hypertrophy work (bodybuilding-
style loading) followed by maximal efforts against heavy loads. Verkhoshansky's own
research is cited as finding the strength deficit increases as external resistance and
movement time decrease, meaning it matters most for fast, low-resistance actions such as
running, jumping, and throwing, and matters less for slow, high-resistance actions. (PDF
p. 21, printed p. 10.)

**Why it works** — A large deficit means there is untapped voluntary/neural capacity
still available, so training that improves recruitment and rate of activation (max effort
or reactive/plyometric methods) has the most room to produce gains. A small deficit means
the athlete is already recruiting close to their ceiling voluntarily, so further gains
require growing the tissue itself (hypertrophy) before neural methods can express more
force.

**When to apply** — Screening question for method selection in explosive/team-sport
athletes: for actions with little time to produce force (change of direction, sprint
push-off, jump takeoff), a large SJ/CMJ-style deficit points toward reactive-strength and
max-effort work over added hypertrophy volume; a small deficit in the same athlete points
toward a hypertrophy or general-strength emphasis instead.

**When NOT to apply** — CAT with 5-8RM loads is not a validated modern method name; treat
it as historical terminology for near-maximal effort training, not a specific protocol to
prescribe as written. Do not use this rule to skip hypertrophy work in an athlete simply
because their sport is "fast" — the size of the individual's own measured deficit, not
the sport category alone, should drive the decision, and no deficit was actually measured
with a validated modern tool.

**Example** — A running back with a large gap between static-start and countermovement
jump height is a better fit for added reactive/plyometric work in that block; a running
back with almost no gap between the two jumps, but comparatively low absolute strength, is
a better fit for a strength/hypertrophy emphasis first.

**Related** — [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]],
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]].

# Rate of Force (or Tension) Development Is a Separate Limiter from Maximal Force

**What it is** — Sporting performance does not depend simply on the ability to produce
maximum force, because many sporting actions happen too fast to recruit an adequate
number of muscle fibres in the available time. Rate of Force Development (RFD) / Rate of
Tension Development (RTD) — how quickly force rises, not just its ceiling — is named as an
independently important limiter, worth assessing on its own alongside maximal-force
deficits. (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10; cross-referenced to 2.2.1 for more detail.)

**Why it works** — Many athletic actions (sprint ground contact, jump takeoff, change of
direction) last far less time than it takes to reach true maximal voluntary force. An
athlete can have high 1RM strength but a slow force-time curve, and still underperform in
short-duration actions, because the task ends before peak force is reached. This
distinction (peak force vs. rate of rise to a sub-maximal time point) is well established
in modern force-time curve analysis, independent of this text.

**When to apply** — Directly supports why Applied Performance tracks driver metrics (e.g.
braking and propulsive force, time-to-peak-force style measures) on ForceDecks rather than
peak force alone, per the department's own output/driver/strategy metric-selection
framework. Use this principle to justify testing and reporting RFD-type variables
separately from 1RM or peak-force values, especially for athletes in short-ground-contact
positions.

**When NOT to apply** — Don't assume RFD and maximal strength always move together, or
that improving one automatically improves the other; they can be trained somewhat
independently (this text develops that further in later chapters on strength-speed and
explosive strength, Ch3, Ch5). Don't substitute a single RFD number for the full force-time
curve when the movement or time window matters (RFD at 0-50ms is a different quality than
RFD at 100-200ms).

**Example** — Two athletes with the same back squat 1RM can produce very different sprint
starts if one reaches a given force threshold in 100ms and the other takes 200ms; testing
and training that difference requires RFD-sensitive measures, not another max-strength
test.

**Related** — [[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]].

# Table 1.1 — Resistance Training Prescription by Goal (Strength, Power, Hypertrophy, Endurance)

**What it is** — A dynamic (non-isometric) resistance-training prescription chart by
goal (PDF p. 22, printed p. 11):

| Variable | Strength | Power | Hypertrophy | Endurance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Load (% 1RM) | 80-100 | 70-100 | 60-80 | 40-60 |
| Reps/set | 1-5 | 1-5 | 8-15 | 25-60 |
| Sets/exercise | 4-7 | 3-5 | 4-8 | 2-4 |
| Rest between sets | 2-6 min | 2-6 min | 2-5 min | 1-2 min |
| Duration/set | 5-10 s | 4-8 s | 20-60 s | 80-150 s |
| Speed/rep (% max) | 60-100 | 90-100 | 60-90 | 60-80 |
| Sessions/week | 3-6 | 3-6 | 5-7 | 8-14 |

High-volume, low-resistance work is called an **extensive** method (an
**extensification/accumulation** phase); low-volume, high-intensity work is an
**intensive** method (an **intensification** phase). Early training typically opens with
an extensive phase before progressing to an intensive one; periodization is described as
cyclically alternating these two phase types.

**Why it works** — Each goal loads the neuromuscular and metabolic systems differently:
near-maximal loads at low reps bias neural recruitment and force capacity (strength);
high-velocity submaximal loads bias rate of force development (power); moderate loads at
moderate-to-high volume bias metabolic and mechanical stress for hypertrophy; light loads
at very high reps bias oxidative/metabolic endurance.

**When to apply** — As a first-pass, generic reference when scoping a new program's
load/volume targets by goal, and as shared vocabulary for extensive/intensive phase
naming when discussing periodization structure with staff or students (HHPR 5355 already
teaches a related undulating volume model).

**When NOT to apply** — The text itself flags this chart as "adequate for the average
personal trainer or coach dealing with the average client or lower level athlete" but
incomplete for advanced athletes: it ignores strength-speed, explosive strength,
flexibility-strength, and strength-endurance as separate qualities, and ignores the many
other prescription variables covered in
[[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]] and later chapters (contraction type,
speed, acceleration profile, rest structure, exercise sequence, agonist/antagonist
balance, individual strength deficit, training and injury history, proficiency level).
Do not use this table as a complete program design tool for a well-trained collegiate
athlete; treat it as a starting reference, not an endpoint.

**Example** — Blocking out approximate set/rep/load ranges for a new hypertrophy-emphasis
mesocycle (60-80% 1RM, 8-15 reps, 4-8 sets) before layering in the athlete-specific
adjustments the text says this table omits.

**Related** — [[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]].

# Beginners Respond to Load Alone; Advanced Athletes Need the Full Variable Set

**What it is** — Load, reps, and sets are described as the traditional core variables of a
weight program, but the text lists a much longer set of variables that matter more as
training age rises: contraction type, movement speed by phase, acceleration at critical
points, rest interval length and type (active/passive), exercise sequence,
agonist/antagonist and stabilizer/mover strength balance, static/dynamic range of motion,
individual strength deficit, training history, injury history, and level of sports
proficiency. The proficiency factor is called out as especially important: exact
sequencing of strength, strength-speed, and hypertrophy work barely matters in a
beginner's first weeks/months but matters a great deal for an experienced athlete. Loads
as small as 40% of 1RM can measurably strengthen a beginner but do nothing for an elite
athlete. (PDF pp. 22-23, printed pp. 11-12.)

**Why it works** — A novice's nervous system and tissue are both far from their adaptive
ceiling, so almost any consistent stimulus produces a training effect; an advanced
athlete has used up most of that low-hanging adaptive room, so the remaining gains depend
on precisely managing the variables that were negligible for the novice.

**When to apply** — As a rule for how much programming detail is worth the coaching time:
spend detailed variable-management effort (sequencing, rest structure, ROM, asymmetry
work) on advanced/experienced athletes, and keep novice programming simple and
consistency-focused rather than over-engineered. Pairs with Bompa's own training-age
framing in this library
([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age|Biological vs Chronological
vs Training Age]]), which makes the same point from the development-model side.

**When NOT to apply** — Don't use "they're a beginner" as an excuse to ignore movement
quality, technique, or safety variables; the simplification applies to programming
complexity (sequencing, minor load percentages), not to coaching attention on how an
exercise is performed. An older athlete new to formal training still has a low training
age and should be treated as a beginner by this rule, not by chronological age.

**Example** — A true freshman gains strength on almost any structured 3x/week program with
straightforward load progression; a fourth-year starter needs exercise sequencing,
recovery structure, and asymmetry correction actively managed to keep progressing.

**Related** — [[framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal]].

# Seven Factors That Limit Strength Production

**What it is** — Strength output in the short and long term is limited by seven
interacting factors: **trainability** (genetic ceiling for hypertrophy, fibre-type
distribution, leverage, and pre-training status); **neuromuscular efficiency** (skill in
recruiting the right muscles accurately and powerfully); **biomechanical efficiency**
(leverage and relative muscle-group strength, trainable unlike raw genetic trainability);
**psychological factors** (motivation, focus, pain tolerance, perceived exertion, coach
influence); **pain and fear of pain** (distinguishing injury pain, a protective signal to
act on, from effort pain, a subjective load-intensity signal usable via an RPE-style
scale); **injury and fear of injury** (reflex inhibition of contraction around a damaged
joint is well documented; return to top performance depends on the athlete's own
perception that rehab is complete, not just medical clearance); and **fatigue** (central
vs. peripheral, discussed further in
[[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]]). (PDF pp. 23-24, printed pp.
12-13.)

**Why it works** — Strength testing and training programs typically control for load,
volume, and technique, but this list makes explicit that psychological state, injury
history, and perceived pain/fear operate as real physiological limiters on force output,
not just "mental" factors layered on top of a physical ceiling — reflex inhibition around
an injured joint is a measurable neuromuscular effect, not a motivation problem.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when an athlete's force output underperforms their
apparent physical capacity: before assuming a physical/programming cause, rule out fear
of re-injury (a documented, not imagined, inhibitor), unaddressed effort-pain tolerance,
or psychological state. Directly relevant to Applied Performance's own RTP framing:
"return to top level performance will occur only if the athlete perceives rehabilitation
to be complete," which is close to a direct match for the department's stated
support role in Athletic Medicine's RTP decisions, and fills part of the gap the method
baseline flags in Rehab/RTP and Injury Risk (thinnest sections in Eric's own corpus).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a descriptive taxonomy, not a measurement protocol; none
of these seven factors have a given cutoff or test threshold in this section. Do not use
"fear of injury" as a catch-all explanation without other supporting evidence (movement
quality, self-report, clinical input from Athletic Medicine); reflex inhibition and
psychological guarding can look similar from the outside.

**Example** — An athlete cleared medically after an ACL reconstruction who still shows
reduced force output on the operated leg during testing may be exhibiting reflex inhibition
and/or fear of re-injury, not a residual physical deficit alone; that changes what the
next intervention should target.

**Related** — [[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]].

# Central vs. Peripheral Fatigue, and Low- vs. High-Frequency Fatigue

**What it is** — Fatigue during short-duration strength/power work is split into
**central fatigue** (reduced motivation, impaired spinal nerve transmission, reduced motor
neuron recruitment and firing rate — a CNS-level phenomenon) and **peripheral fatigue**
(failure somewhere in the excitation-contraction chain at the muscle cell itself: motor
end-plate, sarcolemma, T-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, contractile proteins).
Peripheral fatigue further splits into **low-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at <20 Hz
stimulation, from depressed calcium release, recovering slowly over up to 48 hours) and
**high-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at >50 Hz, recovering faster). "Muscle wisdom"
names the CNS's own down-regulation of motor neuron discharge rate during a sustained
maximal contraction, believed to protect against electrical failure and possibly to
postpone central fatigue. Exercise-induced ammonia accumulation is cited as a possible
contributor to central fatigue at high intensities/durations. Intensive CNS activation
(max weights, max power, plyometrics) is stated to need at least 48 hours of recovery if
no restorative methods are used. (PDF pp. 24-27, printed pp. 13-16.)

**Why it works** — Fatigue is not a single process with one cause; the central/peripheral
split and the frequency-dependent split reflect genuinely different physiological
bottlenecks (nervous drive vs. contractile-machinery failure vs. calcium-handling
kinetics), which is why they have different time courses and respond to different
recovery strategies.

**When to apply** — As the physiological basis for the 48-hour-plus recovery guideline
after maximal-CNS-demand sessions (heavy max effort, plyometrics), which supports spacing
high-CNS-cost sessions (max strength, high-velocity work) at least two days apart within a
microcycle, and for treating "still feels flat two days after a max-effort day" as
plausible central fatigue rather than assuming poor effort or motivation.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a mechanistic taxonomy from exercise physiology, not a
monitoring protocol; none of these fatigue types are directly measured in Applied
Performance's current daily monitoring (mRSI from CMJ is a downstream readiness proxy, not
a direct central/peripheral fatigue assay). Do not over-attribute a flat CMJ day to a
specific named mechanism (e.g., "low-frequency fatigue") without EMG or stimulation data;
in practice, use it only as a conceptual reason why recovery time, not just training
status, should temper interpretation of a single depressed force-plate reading.

**Example** — An athlete who trained max-effort squats yesterday and shows reduced CMJ
output today is more likely showing central/low-frequency fatigue still resolving than a
loss of underlying strength; retesting 48 hours later is more informative than reacting to
the single depressed value.

**Related** — [[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]].

# Strength Expression Depends on Torque Management, Not Just Load

**What it is** — Torque (force times the perpendicular distance from the force's line of
action to the joint fulcrum) determines effective loading on a joint, independent of the
absolute weight lifted. Bringing a load closer to a joint reduces the torque at that
joint for the same weight: flexing the elbows reduces shoulder torque during dumbbell
raises/flyes/bench press; keeping a bar close to the body during the clean or deadlift
reduces torque at the lumbar spine and hips, allowing a heavier load to be lifted more
safely. Swinging the bar away from the body during a snatch pull, or a javelin away from
the shoulder during wind-up, are cited as inefficient uses of torque. (PDF pp. 28-29,
printed pp. 17-18.)

**Why it works** — Torque = force x moment arm; for a fixed external force (a given
weight), shortening the moment arm directly lowers the rotational demand on the joint,
which is standard, independently-established biomechanics, not specific to this text.

**When to apply** — Coaching cue and technical-fault-diagnosis tool for any lift where the
bar or load can drift away from the body's midline (clean, snatch, deadlift, overhead
press) or away from a joint (dumbbell raises, flyes): keeping the load's path close to the
relevant joint is both a safety cue and a load-capacity cue.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a mechanical principle about joint loading, not a
complete safety framework; it does not account for tissue tolerance, technique
proficiency, or fatigue-related form breakdown on its own. Reducing joint torque is not
always desirable if the goal is specifically to overload that joint's musculature for
rehabilitation purposes (e.g., some hip- or shoulder-isolation rehab work intentionally
increases moment arm at a target joint under controlled load).

**Example** — Cueing an athlete to keep the bar against the shins and thighs during a
clean pull, rather than swinging it forward, reduces lumbar torque for the same bar
weight and is both a technique and a load-management fix.

**When to apply** — Justifies programming that targets a specific region of the
force-velocity spectrum rather than assuming "more strength" automatically transfers to
speed: heavy-load, low-velocity work develops the force end; light-load, high-velocity
(including ballistic/plyometric) work develops the velocity end. Use as the conceptual
basis for choosing between a strength-speed or speed-strength emphasis block for an
athlete whose limiter has been identified (e.g., via jump testing or sprint force-velocity
profiling).

**When NOT to apply** — Don't treat "no correlation between max strength and max
velocity" as license to ignore strength training for a speed-limited athlete; a certain
strength floor is still typically necessary before speed-specific training pays off (this
text and others address that sequencing in later chapters, e.g. the Vermeil hierarchy
already used at Baylor: work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed). Note the
text itself flags the classic hyperbolic F-V curve as not universally accurate: research on
the lumbar erector spinae shows a "yielding" drop in force during constant-velocity
eccentric stretching that the standard curve doesn't predict (Sutamo & McGill, 1995) — the
model is a strong generalization, not a universal law for every muscle group.

# The Force-Velocity Relationship, and Why Strength Doesn't Guarantee Speed

**What it is** — Hill's hyperbolic force-velocity curve: velocity of contraction is
inversely related to load; large force cannot be produced at very high velocities under
constant conditions; heavy strength training shifts the curve upward, particularly in
beginners (raising force at all velocities, called training for "strength-speed"); light,
high-velocity training shifts the curve's velocity maximum rightward (called training for
"speed-strength"). Because power = force x velocity, both shifts raise power, just at
different points on the curve. Critically, there is no correlation between an athlete's
maximal strength and their maximal velocity — they are described as different motor
abilities. (PDF pp. 30-31, printed pp. 19-20; Zatsiorsky & Matveev 1964, Komi 1979,
Zatsiorsky 1995.)

**Why it works** — The F-V relationship reflects the cross-bridge cycling and motor unit
recruitment limits of muscle contraction; it has been confirmed for whole-body sporting
movement as well as isolated muscle, and is the direct ancestor of the force-velocity
profiling methods (Samozino, Morin, and others) used in modern sprint and jump testing.

**When to apply** — Justifies programming that targets a specific region of the
force-velocity spectrum rather than assuming "more strength" automatically transfers to
speed: heavy-load, low-velocity work develops the force end; light-load, high-velocity
(including ballistic/plyometric) work develops the velocity end. Use as the conceptual
basis for choosing between a strength-speed or speed-strength emphasis block for an
athlete whose limiter has been identified (e.g., via jump testing or sprint force-velocity
profiling).

**When NOT to apply** — Don't treat "no correlation between max strength and max
velocity" as license to ignore strength training for a speed-limited athlete; a certain
strength floor is still typically necessary before speed-specific training pays off (this
text and others address that sequencing in later chapters, e.g. the Vermeil hierarchy
already used at Baylor: work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed). Note the
text itself flags the classic hyperbolic F-V curve as not universally accurate: research on
the lumbar erector spinae shows a "yielding" drop in force during constant-velocity
eccentric stretching that the standard curve doesn't predict (Sutamo & McGill, 1995) — the
model is a strong generalization, not a universal law for every muscle group.

**Example** — Two athletes with equal back squat 1RM (similar max force) can have very
different unloaded sprint speeds; that gap is F-V curve position, not raw strength, and
argues for velocity-end training (sprint work, light-load ballistics) rather than more
heavy squatting to close it.

**Related** — [[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]],
[[principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods]].

# The Same Force (F = ma) Produced Different Ways Trains Differently

**What it is** — Newton's second law (F = ma) means the same force can be produced with a
large mass and small acceleration (powerlifting-style, heavy load), a small mass and large
acceleration (many track and field actions), a moderate mass and moderate acceleration
(bodybuilding-style hypertrophy training, roughly 8-12 reps), or near-zero acceleration
under isometric/isokinetic conditions. Despite equal force output, these methods are
argued and shown in practice not to produce the same training effect, because different
neural, muscular, and metabolic processes are engaged in each case. (PDF pp. 32-33,
printed pp. 21-22.)

**Why it works** — Force alone does not specify the movement's velocity, duration, muscle
action type, or motor unit recruitment/firing pattern, all of which independently affect
the training stimulus; two efforts that reach the same peak force via different mass-
acceleration combinations are mechanically equal on that one variable but different on
several others that matter physiologically. This is the mechanistic backbone of the
general specificity-of-training principle, which is well established independent of this
text.

**When to apply** — As a reasoning check against choosing exercises solely by "how much
force does this produce," when the intended adaptation (max strength vs. explosive
power vs. hypertrophy vs. isometric endurance) requires matching the mass-acceleration
profile, not just the force magnitude, to the target quality.

**When NOT to apply** — Isokinetic training (option d, F = k.R) is noted to correlate
poorly with actual sporting performance despite being able to produce meaningful
non-specific strength gains in a lab setting; don't treat isokinetic results as a proxy
for how an athlete will perform in ballistic, free-loading sport actions.

**Example** — A powerlifting-style heavy squat and an Olympic-style ballistic
clean pull can both produce a similar peak force at the bar, but the clean pull's high
acceleration under a lighter relative load trains rate of force development and ballistic
coordination that the heavy, slow squat does not, and vice versa for maximal-tension
adaptation.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]].

# A Minimum Load Threshold Drives Strength Gains, and It Rises as the Athlete Adapts

**What it is** — Hettinger & Muller (1953) are cited for a threshold training stimulus of
roughly one-third of maximal strength needed to produce a strength increase in an average
person; as strength rises, the required stimulus intensity rises too, eventually reaching
80-95% of the athlete's maximum, sometimes matching or exceeding actual competition
intensity (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Each stimulus level has its own "strengthening
threshold," a ceiling beyond which no further gain occurs at that intensity, and this
ceiling is described as further from the untrained state the less trained the athlete is.
Separately, Korobkov, Gerasimov & Vasiliev (via Verkhoshansky, 1977) are cited for the
finding that in the initial stages of training, strength increases roughly uniformly
regardless of load, with approximately equivalent gains reported at 20%, 40%, 60% and 80%
of 1RM; raising training intensity early (heavier load, faster tempo, less rest) does not
reliably improve on this until strength has already progressed some way. (PDF pp. 33-34,
printed pp. 22-23.)

**Why it works** — Early neuromuscular adaptation (see
[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]) responds to almost
any sufficiently repeated stimulus above a low floor; once that easy adaptive window
closes, further progress requires a stimulus that approaches the athlete's current
ceiling, because there is less slack left in recruitment and coordination to exploit.

**When to apply** — Supports keeping early-phase (novice) load prescription simple and
consistency-focused rather than chasing high intensities, and supports progressively
raising relative intensity toward 80-95% of max as an athlete's training age increases,
consistent with the training-age-scaling heuristic already noted in this book
([[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]]).

**When NOT to apply** — These are single-source, decades-old figures (Hettinger 1961,
Korobkov et al. via a 1977 secondary citation) without a stated sample or modern
replication in this text; do not treat "one-third of max" or the specific 20/40/60/80%
equivalence as precise, universal cutoffs for a current athlete population. Use them as a
directional argument for why novice programming can be simple, not as exact percentages
to program from.

**Example** — A true beginner's program built around consistent submaximal loading (e.g.
50-60% 1RM) can produce comparable early strength gains to a heavier protocol, so there is
little value in front-loading high intensity before the athlete has trained long enough to
need it.

**Related** — [[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]].

**When to apply** — Conceptual ancestor of today's velocity-based training (VBT) cueing:
"move the bar as fast as possible" instructions on submaximal sets are a direct, modern
implementation of this idea, and map onto the department's existing Perch VBT capability.
Useful coaching language for eccentric-phase control (actively resisting the descent, not
just letting gravity lower the bar) and for isometric holds (actively maintaining
tension rather than assuming a static position is passive).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a technique/cueing concept, not a load-prescription
protocol; it doesn't specify a percentage, velocity target, or rep scheme on its own.
Cueing maximal intended acceleration on every rep is not appropriate for all training
goals (e.g., controlled-tempo hypertrophy work deliberately avoids this).

# Compensatory (Acceleration/Action) Training — Using Proprioceptive Feedback to Actively Manage Bar Speed

**What it is** — Free weights (unlike some variable-resistance machines) let the lifter
feel changing leverage through the range of motion via proprioceptive feedback and respond
by voluntarily accelerating or decelerating the bar to raise or lower the force produced.
This is termed Compensatory Acceleration Training (CAT), most obviously used
concentrically, but the text argues it applies just as much eccentrically (muscles
actively resist gravity's acceleration to control the descent) and even isometrically
(the lifter must continuously compensate for fatigue-driven declines in neural drive to
hold a constant position), leading the author to prefer "Compensatory Action Training" as
the fuller name. (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21; Ch 7.1 develops it further.)

**Why it works** — Because force is not fixed by the weight alone (F = ma; a lighter bar
accelerated hard can still produce meaningful force), an athlete who actively drives bar
speed rather than passively moving a fixed load is directly manipulating the training
stimulus at every point in the range of motion, not just at the load's nominal percentage
of 1RM.

**When to apply** — Conceptual ancestor of today's velocity-based training (VBT) cueing:
"move the bar as fast as possible" instructions on submaximal sets are a direct, modern
implementation of this idea, and map onto the department's existing Perch VBT capability.
Useful coaching language for eccentric-phase control (actively resisting the descent, not
just letting gravity lower the bar) and for isometric holds (actively maintaining
tension rather than assuming a static position is passive).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a technique/cueing concept, not a load-prescription
protocol; it doesn't specify a percentage, velocity target, or rep scheme on its own.
Cueing maximal intended acceleration on every rep is not appropriate for all training
goals (e.g., controlled-tempo hypertrophy work deliberately avoids this).

**Example** — Coaching "explode the bar up" on a submaximal front squat set is applying
CAT: the athlete voluntarily increases bar acceleration beyond what the load alone would
produce, raising the true training force above the load's nominal value.

**Related** — [[principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods]].

# Soviet Sport-School Guideline Ages by Sport (Start, Specialize, Peak)

**What it is** — A per-sport table (Table 1.2) of recommended ages to begin a sport,
begin specialization, and expect high performance, drawn from the Soviet sports-school
system. Examples: basketball 7-8 / 10-12 / 20-25; gymnastics (women) 4-5 / 10-11 / 14-18;
gymnastics (men) 5-6 / 12-14 / 18-24; swimming 3-7 / 10-12 / 16-18; track-and-field 6-7 /
13-14 / 18-23; weightlifting 10-11 / 17-18 / 21-28; wrestling 10-11 / 15-16 / 24-28 (17
sports listed in total). Early, intense specialization is explicitly discouraged in
strength and endurance sports for children; the average age of Soviet Olympians in the
era cited was about 24, with fewer than 10% under age 20. (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp.
24-25.)

**Why it works** — Same underlying rationale as this library's existing long-term
athletic development material: early specialization in strength/endurance sports produces
faster short-term progress but a lower ultimate ceiling and more attrition, because the
young athlete has not built the broad physical base specialization later draws on.

**When to apply** — As a more granular, sport-by-sport reference table alongside this
library's existing LTAD guidance. It converges with, and adds numeric detail beyond, the
Bompa library's
[[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model|Long-Term Sequential Development
Model]], which states a general "not before ~14-15" specialization guideline but does not
break it out by individual sport the way this table does.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a 20th-century Soviet sports-school table, not a modern,
population-representative dataset; individual biological maturation varies (see
[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age|Biological vs Training
Age]]), and American collegiate sport pathways (e.g. football) do not map cleanly onto
these Soviet age bands. Treat the specific ages as illustrative, not prescriptive, for a
Baylor Athletics context.

**Example** — The table's general caution against early strength/endurance specialization
supports keeping a young multi-sport athlete on broad physical preparation rather than
early single-sport strength specialization, consistent with existing LTAD guidance already
in this library.

recommended there: add a line noting Supertraining Table 1.2 gives per-sport numeric ages
that concretize this framework's general specialization-age guidance).

# Strength Training Adapts Along (at Least) Ten Independent, Narrow Dimensions

**What it is** — Strength gains transfer narrowly, not generally, across at least ten
independent dimensions: type of muscle contraction, movement pattern, region/range of
movement, velocity of movement, force of contraction, muscle fibre recruitment,
metabolism, biochemical adaptation, flexibility, and fatigue. Training that improves one
dimension often produces little or no improvement on the others, even when the same
muscle groups are involved. Specificity is explicitly distinguished from simulation:
mimicking a sport movement with added resistance is not the same as training the specific
factors above, and can actually distort the neuromuscular programming needed for the real
skill because of changes in center of gravity, moment of inertia, and mechanical
stiffness introduced by the resistance. (PDF pp. 38-39, printed pp. 27-28.)

**Why it works** — Strength adaptation is produced and expressed by the nervous and
muscular systems together (see
[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]); the specific
demands (velocity, joint angle, contraction type, metabolic pathway) shape which
recruitment patterns, fibre types, and biochemical pathways are trained, so a change in
any one of those parameters can produce a materially different, largely non-transferable
adaptation. This is one of the more broadly replicated findings in strength and
conditioning research, independent of this text.

**When to apply** — As the master reasoning check before assuming an exercise "transfers"
to a sport skill: ask which of the ten dimensions the exercise actually matches (velocity,
region of movement, contraction type, etc.), not just whether it uses similar muscles.
Directly supports Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky, Ch4.3), already taught in HHPR
5355 and part of Eric's baseline, as the applied extension of this same specificity logic
to exercise selection.

**When NOT to apply** — Don't use "specificity" as an argument against any general
preparation work; the text elsewhere (1.1, and the department's own multilateral/LTAD
material) supports building a general base before narrowing to sport-specific work. This
principle governs which dimensions transfer, not whether general work has value at an
earlier training age.

**Example** — Heavy squat strength does not automatically transfer to high-velocity sprint
force production (different point on the velocity dimension) even though both use similar
musculature; each needs its own specific training exposure.

**Related** — [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]],
[[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]].

# High-Velocity Training Transfers to Low Velocity Better Than the Reverse; Contraction Modes Barely Cross Over

**What it is** — Two specific, cited findings under the specificity umbrella: (1)
low-velocity isokinetic training improves low-velocity strength but has minimal effect on
high-velocity strength; high-velocity isokinetic training improves high-velocity strength
and transfers somewhat better to low-velocity strength than the reverse direction
(Moffroid & Whipple 1970; Perrine & Edgerton 1981; Kanehisa & Miyashita 1983b). (2)
Contraction-mode adaptations are narrow: concentric-eccentric (weightlifting-style)
training raises competitive strength but produces only small isometric or concentric
isokinetic gains; isometric training raises isometric strength but not concentric
isokinetic strength; elbow-extension training with weights increases triceps strength and
girth without a matching isokinetic-strength change. Static and dynamic training even
produce different microscopic structural changes in the muscle. (PDF pp. 38-40, printed
pp. 27-29.)

**Why it works** — Force-velocity curve position (see
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]) and contraction-mode
recruitment patterns are trained narrowly because different neural drive strategies and
structural adaptations underlie each; high-velocity training likely also recruits fast-
twitch units that contribute somewhat at slower speeds, which is the proposed reason the
transfer is asymmetric rather than symmetric.

**When to apply** — When selecting exercise velocity and contraction mode, match both to
the sport action being targeted, and bias toward including higher-velocity work when in
doubt, since it transfers in both directions somewhat, whereas slow, heavy work transfers
poorly to fast actions. Use as a rationale for including isometric mid-thigh pull or
isometric testing/training (already part of Baylor's ForceDecks protocol) as its own
distinct quality, not a proxy for dynamic 1RM strength.

**When NOT to apply** — These are 1970s-1980s isokinetic-dynamometer studies; isokinetic
machine training is a narrow, lab-style modality rarely used in current collegiate S&C
practice, and this specific transfer asymmetry has not been independently re-verified here
for free-weight or plyometric training modes. Do not assume the same asymmetric-transfer
ratio applies to, say, barbell velocity-based training without separate evidence.

**Example** — An athlete tested for isometric mid-thigh pull strength should not be assumed
to have an equivalent dynamic 1RM or sprint force capability; each needs its own
assessment and, if targeted, its own specific training exposure.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]].

# The Bilateral Deficit: Two Limbs Together Produce Less Force Than the Sum of Each Alone

**What it is** — Force produced during a bilateral (two-limb, e.g. barbell) contraction is
usually less than the sum of the forces each limb produces individually (e.g. dumbbells),
a phenomenon called the bilateral deficit, accompanied by reduced integrated EMG
suggesting the prime movers are less activated bilaterally (Coyle et al. 1981;
Vandervoort et al. 1984). The deficit is reported as insignificant in athletes who always
use their limbs simultaneously in their sport (e.g. weightlifters), and the text
recommends athletes whose sport involves bilateral action of the same muscle groups train
bilaterally to minimize the deficit (Secher, 1975). (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28.)

**Why it works** — The deficit is attributed to a neural, not mechanical, limitation:
reduced activation of the prime movers during simultaneous bilateral effort, which
training the specific bilateral pattern appears to reduce over time — another instance of
narrow, mode-specific neuromuscular adaptation.

**When to apply** — When deciding whether to prioritize bilateral (back squat, bench,
clean) or unilateral (split squat, single-leg press, lunge) exercise variants: match the
training mode to how the sport actually loads the limbs. For sports with genuinely
unilateral force production (sprinting, most cutting and change-of-direction actions),
this argues for meaningful unilateral training exposure, not exclusively bilateral lifts,
since bilateral-only training may under-develop the single-limb activation football and
track actions actually require.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this to argue against bilateral lifts altogether;
compound bilateral lifts remain valuable for maximal strength and are appropriate where
the sport itself uses bilateral effort (e.g. some blocking or lifting actions). The
deficit's size and trainability likely vary by athlete and lift, and no specific
magnitude is given in this text for team-sport athletes.

**Example** — A sprinter's single-leg force production during ground contact is not fully
predicted by their bilateral back squat strength alone; programming that includes
single-leg strength work targets the bilateral deficit gap directly relevant to sprint and
change-of-direction performance.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]].

39	
40	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states isokinetic training (option d, F = k.R)
41	correlates poorly with actual sporting performance despite producing meaningful
42	non-specific strength gains in a lab setting (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22, citing Rosentzweig
43	& Hinson 1972, Ostemig 1986). **Inference:** don't treat isokinetic results as a proxy for
44	how an athlete will perform in ballistic, free-loading sport actions; this specific
45	caution is this entry's own restatement of that finding's practical implication.

47	**Example** — **Inference:** A powerlifting-style heavy squat and an Olympic-style ballistic
48	clean pull can both produce a similar peak force at the bar, but the clean pull's high
49	acceleration under a lighter relative load trains rate of force development and ballistic
50	coordination that the heavy, slow squat does not, and vice versa for maximal-tension
51	adaptation.
