Our discussion of bioenergetics commenced with a definition of fitness. It is now appropriate to examine the 
implications of the above information for enhancing some of the components which underlie fitness: strength, 
muscular endurance, speed and cardiovascular endurance. The preceding analysis reveals that the development of 
a specific fitness component depends on adjusting the intensity, duration and type of training. In general, power 
and strength rely heavily on the high energy phosphagen system, muscle endurance on the oxygen-independent 
glycolytic system, and cardiovascular endurance on the oxygen-dependent energy system.
The single maximal muscular contractions characteristic of maximal power developed over a period which 
may last a fraction of a second rely entirely on stored ATP. This process does not increase blood lactate levels 
and the limitation to continued effort lies largely in the availability of ATP.
After a few seconds, CP is drawn upon to replenish the rapidly dwindling ATP. The CP contribution 
reaches a peak after 5-7 seconds, during which time oxygen-independeni glycolysis  has already commenced (Fig 
1J7). Extraction of energy from the CP system also does not cause a build-up of lactate and protons, so that the 
main limitation to continued effort is the availability of the enzyme (creatine kinase) which resynthcsizes ATP
79


===== PDF 91 =====
SUPERTRAINING
(Fig 1.35). Maximal force development no longer becomes possible and muscle endurance becomes the dominant 
fitness component.
Figure 1.37 The contribution of the different energy systems to maximal exercise of increasing duration (based on van Handel & Puhl
Clinics in Sports Medicine 1983, 2: 19-30)
Strenuous exercise lasting between approximately 6-30 seconds activates oxygen-independent glycolysis 
maximally, but appropriate rest intervals will prevent a serious increase in blood lactate. This is the rationale 
behind the value of interval and fartlek (repeated jog-sprint) running, and interval circuit training with weights or

# Classic Energy-System Percentage Tables by Sport (Fox & Mathews, 1974) — Football Listed at ~90% Phosphagen

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky reproduces Fox & Mathews' (1974) classic tables estimating
the percentage contribution of the short-term (phosphagen/ATP-CP), intermediate
(non-oxidative glycolytic), and long-term (oxidative/aerobic) energy systems to different
training modes and sports. American football is listed at 90% short-term, 10%
intermediate, 0% long-term — among the most phosphagen-dominant sports in the table,
comparable to golf (95/5/0) and volleyball (90/10/0), and far more phosphagen-dominant
than field hockey or soccer half-backs (60/20/20). Verkhoshansky himself cautions that
this "highly determinate" scheme, compiled decades earlier, has been questioned, that
figures for some events (he names the 1500m specifically) have since been revised, and
that it should not be used casually because it disguises moment-to-moment metabolic
demand shifts within a single sport. (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81.)

**Why it works** — The table estimates an average, whole-game contribution, whereas actual
play consists of short high-intensity bursts (plays) separated by long rest (huddles,
substitutions), so an average figure can obscure the real repeated-sprint, phosphagen-
dominant-per-play structure while also underweighting the role of aerobic recovery between
bursts.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's stated conditioning priority for
football is alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp and game demands, with
glycolytic conditioning treated as a "worst case scenario" absorbed incidentally rather
than programmed as a primary target (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39`); the baseline also states the aerobic
system's main value for speed-power athletes is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP
between bouts), not distance capacity (citing `2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md
p.9`). **Inference:** this table's 90/10/0 split for football (near-zero credited to the
long-term/aerobic system) looks, at first read, to be in tension with the baseline's
explicit inclusion of aerobic capacity as a Goal-1 priority for football — but the tension
likely resolves once "aerobic system" is understood functionally: the baseline treats
aerobic fitness as enabling faster ATP/phosphagen regeneration between the very
phosphagen-dominant plays this table describes, not as a source of in-play energy. Read
together, not as contradictory: this table describes what fuels a single play; the
baseline describes what determines how well that fuel regenerates for the next one.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky's own caution applies directly here: **Inference**
do not use the 90/10/0 football figure as a precise or current number; it is a decades-old
average estimate for the sport as a whole, not a modern, position-specific or play-by-play
breakdown, and the source text itself flags the whole table's accuracy as needing
re-examination. This entry is rated `contested` because it is presented as a classic,
already-questioned scheme rather than an established modern reference.

**Example** — **Inference:** a single football play (a few seconds of maximal effort)
draws almost entirely on the phosphagen system, consistent with the table; but the
athlete's ability to repeat that near-maximal output play after play, series after series,
depends heavily on aerobic capacity for recovery between plays — the quality the baseline
prioritizes.

**Related** — None in this ingest yet; candidate future link to a conditioning synthesis
note once Phase 4 of the Flint project reaches conditioning and energy systems.

# Lactate Does Not "Poison" Muscle or Cause Soreness; "Oxygen Debt" Is an Outdated Concept

**What it is** — Two corrections to common misconceptions. (1) Muscle fatigue is not due
to "lactic acid poisoning"; lactate formation is accompanied by hydrogen ions that increase
acidity and can interfere with contraction and enzyme efficiency, but lactate itself is not
the toxin popularly described, and blood lactate returns to normal within about an hour of
strenuous interval training — well before delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically
peaks. The most pronounced soreness actually occurs after prolonged endurance efforts kept
below the lactate threshold, so current theory attributes soreness to transient muscle
cell or connective tissue damage, not lactic acid. (2) The classic "oxygen debt" concept
(the idea that post-exercise heavy breathing "repays" an oxygen deficit incurred during
anaerobic work) is now considered outdated; the post-exercise period instead reflects
recovery oxygen consumption used to regenerate ATP and CP and restore respiratory, ionic,
circulatory, hormonal, and thermal systems to baseline (McArdle, Katch & Katch, 1991). The
older term "anaerobic threshold" has similarly been replaced by "blood lactate threshold"
or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation) since lactate does not require an absence of
oxygen to form. (PDF pp. 87, 89, printed pp. 76, 78.)

**Why it works** — Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise
physiology: lactate is a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not an anaerobic waste
product to be "cleared" or "repaid," and glycolysis runs alongside oxidative metabolism
rather than only replacing it when oxygen is absent (also noted in this book: glycolysis
dominates during sprinting even though muscles have adequate oxygen).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for correcting persistent coaching-room and
classroom misconceptions (e.g. in HHPR 5355 teaching) — "lactic acid causes the burn and
next-day soreness" and "you're paying back oxygen debt after a sprint" are both outdated
framings that this entry can directly correct with citable sources.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** correcting the mechanism does not mean lactate is
irrelevant to training; the blood lactate threshold (OBLA) remains a legitimate, useful
marker for endurance training intensity and athlete conditioning status — only the
"lactic acid as toxin/soreness cause" framing and the "oxygen debt" framing are being
corrected here, not the practical value of lactate-threshold-based training zones.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete sore two days after a hard endurance session is
more likely dealing with muscle/connective tissue microtrauma than residual lactate, which
would have cleared within an hour; recovery guidance should be based on that, not on
"flushing out lactic acid."

**Related** — [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]].

or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation) since lactate does not require an absence of
oxygen to form. (PDF pp. 87, 89, printed pp. 76, 78.)

**Why it works** — Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise
physiology: lactate is a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not an anaerobic waste
product to be "cleared" or "repaid," and glycolysis runs alongside oxidative metabolism
rather than only replacing it when oxygen is absent (also noted in this book: glycolysis
dominates during sprinting even though muscles have adequate oxygen).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for correcting persistent coaching-room and
classroom misconceptions (e.g. in HHPR 5355 teaching) — "lactic acid causes the burn and
next-day soreness" and "you're paying back oxygen debt after a sprint" are both outdated
framings that this entry can directly correct with citable sources.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** correcting the mechanism does not mean lactate is
irrelevant to training; the blood lactate threshold (OBLA) remains a legitimate, useful
marker for endurance training intensity and athlete conditioning status — only the
"lactic acid as toxin/soreness cause" framing and the "oxygen debt" framing are being
corrected here, not the practical value of lactate-threshold-based training zones.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete sore two days after a hard endurance session is
more likely dealing with muscle/connective tissue microtrauma than residual lactate, which
would have cleared within an hour; recovery guidance should be based on that, not on
"flushing out lactic acid."

**Related** — [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]].

SUPERTRAINING
Thus, although Table 1.4 indicates that endurance events such as distance running, swimming and cross 
country skiing rely largely on the long-term energy system, there arc stages of acceleration and increased muscular 
effort which make significant demands on the short-term ‘anaerobic’ and the intermediate energy systems, 
Moreover, while we may consider that the body as a whole or the cardiocirculatory and respiratory systems may 
be relying largely on ‘aerobic* processes, we cannot ignore that strongly contracting postural and propulsive 
muscles may be strongly dependent upon ‘anaerobic’ processes at the same time. The implications of this arc 
that exercise prescription should not rely on the analysis of just one aspect of sporting performance. Therefore, it 
would be logical to include some regular bouts of high intensity and high speed training even for so-called 
endurance sports.
The duration of this exercise depends ultimately on the amount of glycogen stored in the liver and skeletal 
musclcs, as well as the efficiency of deriving energy from fatty acids. Glycogen storage may be enhanced by 
means of'carbo-loading', which relies on a few days of moderate carbohydrate depletion followed by the large 
intake of complex carbohydrates before a major event in order to promote some glycogen super compensation.
Research shows that the rate of glycogen synthesis after endurance exercise is strongly influenced by the 
timing of carbohydrate ingestion (Ivy et al, 1988). It was discovered that drinking a 23% carbohydrate solution 
(2gm per kilogram of bodymass) instead of water directly after exercise produced a 300% increase in the rate of 
glycogen synthesis above the basal rate during the first two hours of recovery. A delay in carbohydrate ingestion 
by only two hours resulted in a 47% slower rate of resynthesis.
This emphasizes that efficient physical conditioning is a consequence of balanced nutrition combined with an 
exercise schedule of appropriate intensity, duration and type, carefully periodiscd over a prolonged period which 
includes suitable restoration phases to regenerate energy stores, repair the cells and promote regular 
supcrcompensation.
1.15.7 Hormonal Factors and Strength Training
Both acute and long-term exercise influence the endocrine system, with decreases in testosterone levels being 
measured in distance athletes and increases occurring among certain athletes using resistance training (see review 
by Terjung, 1979). The implications of such findings are of importance to strength and hypertrophy training, 
since both of these factors are positively affected by the levels of growth-promoting substances, such as 
testosterone, in the blood. This is the main reason why the abuse of artificial anabolic agents is so widespread in 
sport today.
Some studies of training programmes have yielded equivocal results, largely because of the difficulty in 
prescribing the exercise precisely in terms of intensity, volume, rest periods and long-term periodisation. Short­
term strength training has been shown to produce no changes in the level of anabolic-androgenic hormones in the 
body (Young et al, 1976; Hetrick & 

===== PDF 94 =====
SUPERTRAINING
achicvc a specific type of fitness. Here it must be noted that the concept of fitness is not the only one relating to 
the ability of an athlete to perform efficiently and safely. One has to distinguish between the related factors of 
h< ork capacity, fitness and preparedness , as introduced earlier (1.4). Training and environmental factors affect all 
of these abilities and the models discussed here relate to all of them.
As was discussed earlier (1.3), training is highly specific to the methods being used, a fact which has been 
formulated as the well-known SAID principle  (Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demands). Simply stated, this 
means that the body adapts with a specific type of fitness to any demands which may be regularly imposed on it, 
provided the loading does not exceed the adaptive capabilities of the body at that time.
The Effects of Stress
The nature and effects of stress were extensively researched by Hans Selye, who devised a comprehensive model 
to describe the response of living systems to sources of stress (stressors) in the environment (Selye, 1956). This 
model, which he termed the General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS),  has been widely used to explaining the process 
of strength development and is summarised here mainly because of its historical significance and its early impact 
on training theory. Selye identified two forms of stress: eustress , beneficial stress which produces growth, and 
distress, detrimental stress which can cause decay, damage, death or disease (Fig 1.38).
Figure 1J8 The different types of stress and their possible consequences (after Selye)
Well-planned training is characterised by the continued operation of eustress processes, whereas stagnation, 
soreness and persistent minor injuries are early indicators of distress. Later we will see that the Two-Factor  
Model of Training would describe this process as a consequence of the situation where the fatigue factor tends to 
be outweigh the fitness factor over prolonged periods (1.16.3).
Although Selye's model has been applied more recently to explain sports adaptation and supercompensation, 
the concept of supercompensation (Weigert’s Law) was formulated at least a decade before Selye's work (Folbrot, 
1941). Moreover, the relationship between adaptation and exhaustion-recovery processes under different types 
of loading was researched in the early 1950s by Yakovlev (1955).
1.16.1 The General Adaptation Syndrome
Selye's theory postulates that all animals exposed to periods of stress undergo three phases of the GAS: initial 
alarm, resistance and exhaustion. The energy for resistance or adaptation comes from the readily available 
superficial adaptation energy source or the emergency deep adaptation energy  source, depending on the level of 
exhaustion or depletion of energy at any instant. In Russian texts, the former energy source is referred to as the 
Current Adaptation Reserves (CAR),  a term which is used extensively in later sections of this text. The capacity 
of these reserves is not fixed, but alters in response to the demands placed on them by stresses such as training. 
The importance of this will become clear when the conce

===== PDF 95 =====
SUPERTRAINING
Strength training would then refer to training which enables the body to increase the general strength output 
of its muscles, with similar definitions being applicable to all the different types of training. Strength-related 
forms of fitness require the body to competently resist high intensities of stress at a particular time, whereas 
endurance-related forms of fitness require it to withstand lower intensities of stress over prolonged periods.
Research and experience in sport indicate that the GAS model has to be modified to account for the fact that 
training (i.e. planned exposure to specific stressors) can allow one to adapt to increasingly higher levels of stress 
due to various structural and functional changes. This is what is referred to as progressive overload.  However, it 
is inappropriate to apply this principle literally, since research has revealed that optimal progress is made if the  
increased loading phases are alternated periodically with decreased loading phases  (see Ch 6). Continual 
monotonic (non-decreasing) increases from workout to workout or week to week may lead to overtraining, 
stagnation or injury. It is vital to remember that tissue repair and growth occur predominantly during the 
restoration and transition periods between training sessions and not during the heavy loading phases.
It has also been deduced that adaptive processes apparently do not just constrain bodily processes to always 
produce the same, predetermined maximal level of resistance. It has been hypothesised that they cause the body 
to over-adapt, or supercompensate , to a somewhat higher level, in physiological anticipation of repeated exposure 
to the same stressor (Fig 1.39).
This supercompensation is associated with an increase in the capacity of the Current Adaptation Reserves 
(CAR) and forms the foundation for all methods of programming training (Ch 6). At the nutritional level, the 
well-known method of increasing bodily stores of glycogen with significantly increased intake of carbohydrates 
after an exhausting stage of aerobic training may be termed 'glycogen supercompensation'. Unlike the process of 
fitness improvement, successive periods of'carbo loading* do not produce progressively increased storage of 
glycogen. It should also be noted that enhanced performance is not simply the result o f increased stores of  
bioenergetic substances, but also of structural changes in muscle and other tissues , as well as enhanced efficiency 
and rates of bioenergetic and neuromuscular processing (see 1.12). This is a major reason why Russian scientists 
prefer to use the term adaptive reconstruction  to describe the body’s response to physical training.
Figure U 9  Selye’s General Adaptation Syndrome model. The Deep Adaptation Energy is often referred to as the Current Adaptation 
Reserves (CAR) by Russian authors.
Despite these shortcomings, this theory of supercompensation had a profound impact on sports training, since it 
could readily be related to the system of carefully planned cyclical conditioning known as periodisation  (Ch 6). In 
brief, periodisation involves organising all components of training (such as strength,

===== PDF 96 =====
SUPERTRAINING
Adaptive Reconstruction versus Supercompensation
A s emphasized earlier, it is preferable to use a term such as adaptive reconstruction,  rather than 
supcrcompensation when referring to adaptation to training loads by the body. Thus, although the energy 
systems or adaptation reserves would appear to have superadapted, supercompensated or overcompensated in 
magnitude, there are trophic and many other changes elicited by training which are not directly related to changes 
in size of energy stores. Training induced changes in muscle tissue (1.12 and 1.13) and connective tissue (1.7.2) 
such as increased tissue hypertrophy, altered muscle fibre characteristics, intensified protein synthesis, stimulated 
enzyme activity, activation of the genetic apparatus of muscle cells and increased rate of energy release have 
already been discussed. More of these changes will be examined in greater detail in the following section to enable 
us to present other models of training later in this book.
1.16.2 The Biochemistry of Adaptation in Sport
Adaptation is primarily dependent on the interrelation between a cell's function and its genetic apparatus, which 
constitutes the constantly active mechanism of intracellular regulation.
Unlike immediate adaptation reactions, the process of prolonged adaptation to systematic muscular activity 
typically involves significant intensification of the biosynthetic processes, primarily those of protein synthesis, 
as well as the emergence of marked structural changes in the tissues.
The use of radioactively labelled amino acids has revealed that training intensifies the synthesis of proteins in 
the myofibrils, mitochondria, sarcoplasm, and microsomcs of the skeletal muscles and the heart (Platonov, 1988). 
The synthesis of DNA and RNA precursors also intensifies, indicating activation of the genetic apparatus of the 
muscle cell, while RNA synthesis in the cardiac muscle also increases during training. In this respect there is 
increased activity of enzymes which are structural components in the synthesis of nucleic acids.
Training intensifies the formation of all cellular material including the mitochondria, myofibrillar proteins, 
endoplasmic reticulum and various enzymes. The motoneurons also thicken, and the number of terminal nerve 
shoots increases, as docs the number of nuclei and myofibrils in the muscle fibres. In addition to the intensified 
synthesis of structural proteins, synthesis of enzymatic proteins (especially skeletal-muscle aspartate-amino- 
transferase) is increased during training.
The nucleotides (ADP, AMP - adenosine monophosphate), creatine, inorganic phosphate, and some amino 
acids, as well as the ADP/ATP and the creatine/CP ratios, play an important role in activating protein synthesis 
elicited by training. It appears that the accumulation of metabolites formed during muscle activity, as well as the 
decreased ATP and CP levels, might signal activation of the genetic apparatus of the muscle cells. The change in 
the metabolism of hormones such as glucocorticoids, somatotropin, androgens, insulin and the thyroid hormones 
is very important in intensifying protein synthesis durin

===== PDF 97 =====
SUPERTRAINING
The Sequence of Biochemical Changes during Training
The many biochemical changes that take place in the body during and after training (as well as overtraining) do not 
occur simultaneously. A definite sequence in the biochemical adaptation to training is discerned (Platonov, 1988). 
First, the potential for oxidative resynthesis of ATP and the level of glycogen increase. Next there is an increase in 
the level of structural protein in the muscles (myosin) and in the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis 
(glycolysis), following which the level of CP rises.
In overtraining the typical changes of biochemical adaptation acquired through training are gradually lost and 
work capacity decreases. The biochemical indices during overtraining change in an order that is the reverse of the 
order seen during training. Naturally, the dynamics of developing and losing the biochemical changes of 
adaptation depend on the characteristics of the previous training. In general, the longer the training period, the 
more thorough is the reorganisation by the adaptation mechanisms and the longer the accompanying biochemical 
changes last in the body after cessation of training, especially regarding glycogen and CP levels. Thus, the 
biochemical changes during immediate and long-term adaptation to systematic muscle activity are reversible, with 
the process of direct and reverse development of these changes being heterochronic.
During overtraining, the chemistry of the muscles and, above all, the oxidative processes are disturbed. Here 
the glycogenolytic activity of the muscle tissue diminishes, and levels of ascorbic acid, glutathione, and glycogen 
in it decrease (Platonov, 1988). Dysproteinaemia of the blood plasma is noted, and the blood levels of 
glycoproteins, sialic acids, and urea increase. With prolonged chronic fatigue, athletes have reduced functional 
potential of the sympathico-adrenal system, which is closely linked to a disruption of the acid-base balance.
When training loads exceed the adaptation potential of the body and cause fatigue, another type of 
sympathetic nervous system reaction takes place: in fatiguing endurance events, a physical load that was 
previously of relatively little significance for the athletes causes a sharp increase in the excretion of 
catecholamines, their biological precursors, and the products of degradation, i.e. a particular hormonal reaction to 
the test load occurs. It is clear, then that the above-mentioned biochemical changes during overtraining exert an 
unfavourable influence on work capacity and the level of sports results.
The biochemical rules governing bodily adaptation may be used to verify various principles of sports training 
such as the continuity of the training process, the undulatory nature of load dynamics, the cyclical nature of the 
training process, the unity of general and special preparation, the gradual increase in loading and the progression 
toward maximal loading.
A single physical load can cause an immediate biochemical effect, but this rapidly subsides. If a subsequent 
physical load is performed after the traces of the adaptation effect of the first load have compl

===== PDF 98 =====
SUPERTRAINING
All of these changes are closely related to nutrition. The increased energy expenditure during muscle activity 
demands adequate replenishment; increase in need for vitamins demands an increased intake of them; and increased 
mineral losses during sports activity necessitate compensating for them.
A number of other specific problems also arise: nutrition over a long period and during restoration stages; the 
athlete's feeding frequency; and the application of biologically-enriched sports nutrition products. Planning diets 
for athletes also requires a new approach to organising nutrition at different stages of the annual cycle of training 
and competitions, especially concerning the quantities of food components, the interaction between different 
nutrients and optimal timing of ingestion of specific substances (chrononutrition). We must achieve the maximal 
correspondence between all the goals of sports training and the effect of diet on the body. In this respect, the 
biochemical processes underlying sports training form the theoretical basis for scientific sports nutrition.
1.16.3 General Theories of the Training Process
It has been stated previously that almost any regimen of resistance training can be successful with a novice, but in 
the long term, the body habituates to the stimulus, progress slows down and halts as stagnation sets in and 
performance deteriorates (Fig 1.40).
Figure 1.40 The effect of random, casual resistance training over the long term
The gains in strength are rapid during the first few months, a period of several months of fairly stable performance 
follows, until stagnation ensues, especially if there is unskilled use of progressive loading and inadequate training 
variety. Finally, the individual becomes unable to maintain sufficient motivation and central nervous stimulation 
to make further progress. This entire process of adaptation or failure to adapt to physical training has been 
explained by two theoretical models:
• Single-Factor Model of Training (The Supercompensation Model)
• Two-Factor Model of Training (The Fitncss-Fatigue Model)
Single-Factor Model of Training
The single-factor model may be better understood in the light of Selye's GAS model, which provides a theoretical 
foundation for the principle of supercompensation  (Fig 1.41), whereby bodily processes are hypothesised to 
adapt to a higher level of functioning in response to the repeated physical stresses of training. The immediate 
after-effect of training is assumed to deplete certain biochemicals whose amount increases above their initial levels 
during the training period. If subsequent loading is imposed too soon during the recovery stage (at point A), then 
supercompensation fails to occur and performance continues to decrease (Fig 1.41 b).
If a conservative approach is followed and successive bouts of loading are too infrequent or imposed too late 
(at point C), then supercompensation is minimal and performance tends to stagnate (Fig 1.41c). Loading is 
optimal if it is imposed when supercompensation has peaked (at point B); this enables the load to be increased 
regularly without causing stagnation or overloading (Fig 1.

===== PDF 99 =====
SUPERTRAINING
been shown to deplete significantly, even after very strenuous exercise. No supercompensation has yet been 
observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals involved in the various bioenergctic processes in the body. 
Moreover, return to their initial levels by each of these substances after changes have been elicited by physical 
stress takes a different period of time, so the timing of subsequent loads to stimulate the appropriate type of 
supercompcnsation remains indeterminate.
Figure 1.41 Application of the principle of supercompensation for producing optimal training
In addition, various other structural and biochemical factors relating to the adaptation of the body to training have 
been discussed in the previous section. These problems with simple supercompensation theory have led to 
increased criticism and decreased popularity in applying it to explain the training process.
Two-Factor Model of Training
The Two-Factor Model  (or Fitness-Fatigue Model) of the training process involves the superimposition of two 
after-effects following the application of a training load (see 6.7 and especially Figure 6.14), as alluded to earlier in 
the work of Yakovlev (see 1.16):
• A long-term fitness after-effect  which leads to an increase in specific fitness
• A short-term fatigue after-effect  producing a specific type of fatigue
These after-effects interact to produce what is termed physical preparedness.  The first factor is slow-changing 
and longer lasting, leading to progressive, delayed increases in physical fitness, whereas the fatigue after-effect is a 
shorter-lasting negative factor that decreases preparedness (Fig 1.42).
The fatigue effect, though relatively short in duration, displays a greater magnitude than the fitness effect 
Preparedness  at a given time, P(t), is the initial preparedness P(0) before the workout plus the increase in 
preparedness, AP, produced by the summation of the fitness and fatigue after-effects (Fig 1.42). Research has 
described the fitness-fatigue relationship in terms of equations such as the following (Banister et al, 1992):
Preparedness at a time t = Initial Preparedness + Change in Preparedness due to one workout

by Terjung, 1979). The implications of such findings are of importance to strength and hypertrophy training, 
since both of these factors are positively affected by the levels of growth-promoting substances, such as 
testosterone, in the blood. This is the main reason why the abuse of artificial anabolic agents is so widespread in 
sport today.

prescribing the exercise precisely in terms of intensity, volume, rest periods and long-term periodisation. Short­

formulated as the well-known SAID principle  (Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demands). Simply stated, this 
means that the body adapts with a specific type of fitness to any demands which may be regularly imposed on it,

The nature and effects of stress were extensively researched by Hans Selye, who devised a comprehensive model

of strength development and is summarised here mainly because of its historical significance and its early impact 
on training theory. Selye identified two forms of stress: eustress , beneficial stress which produces growth, and 
distress, detrimental stress which can cause decay, damage, death or disease (Fig 1.38).

be outweigh the fitness factor over prolonged periods (1.16.3).

of loading was researched in the early 1950s by Yakovlev (1955).

Adaptation is primarily dependent on the interrelation between a cell's function and its genetic apparatus, which 
constitutes the constantly active mechanism of intracellular regulation.
Unlike immediate adaptation reactions, the process of prolonged adaptation to systematic muscular activity

as well as the emergence of marked structural changes in the tissues.
The use of radioactively labelled amino acids has revealed that training intensifies the synthesis of proteins in 
the myofibrils, mitochondria, sarcoplasm, and microsomcs of the skeletal muscles and the heart (Platonov, 1988). 
The synthesis of DNA and RNA precursors also intensifies, indicating activation of the genetic apparatus of the

work capacity decreases. The biochemical indices during overtraining change in an order that is the reverse of the 
order seen during training. Naturally, the dynamics of developing and losing the biochemical changes of

more thorough is the reorganisation by the adaptation mechanisms and the longer the accompanying biochemical

the process of direct and reverse development of these changes being heterochronic.
During overtraining, the chemistry of the muscles and, above all, the oxidative processes are disturbed. Here 
the glycogenolytic activity of the muscle tissue diminishes, and levels of ascorbic acid, glutathione, and glycogen 
in it decrease (Platonov, 1988). Dysproteinaemia of the blood plasma is noted, and the blood levels of 
glycoproteins, sialic acids, and urea increase. With prolonged chronic fatigue, athletes have reduced functional 
potential of the sympathico-adrenal system, which is closely linked to a disruption of the acid-base balance.

sympathetic nervous system reaction takes place: in fatiguing endurance events, a physical load that was 
previously of relatively little significance for the athletes causes a sharp increase in the excretion of 
catecholamines, their biological precursors, and the products of degradation, i.e. a particular hormonal reaction to 
the test load occurs. It is clear, then that the above-mentioned biochemical changes during overtraining exert an 
unfavourable influence on work capacity and the level of sports results.

such as the continuity of the training process, the undulatory nature of load dynamics, the cyclical nature of the 
training process, the unity of general and special preparation, the gradual increase in loading and the progression 
toward maximal loading.

physical load is performed after the traces of the adaptation effect of the first load have compl

All of these changes are closely related to nutrition. The increased energy expenditure during muscle activity 
demands adequate replenishment; increase in need for vitamins demands an increased intake of them; and increased 
mineral losses during sports activity necessitate compensating for them.
A number of other specific problems also arise: nutrition over a long period and during restoration stages; the 
athlete's feeding frequency; and the application of biologically-enriched sports nutrition products. Planning diets 
for athletes also requires a new approach to organising nutrition at different stages of the annual cycle of training 
and competitions, especially concerning the quantities of food components, the interaction between different 
nutrients and optimal timing of ingestion of specific substances (chrononutrition). We must achieve the maximal 
correspondence between all the goals of sports training and the effect of diet on the body. In this respect, the 
biochemical processes underlying sports training form the theoretical basis for scientific sports nutrition.
1.16.3 General Theories of the Training Process
It has been stated previously that almost any regimen of resistance training can be successful with a novice, but in 
the long term, the body habituates to the stimulus, progress slows down and halts as stagnation sets in and 
performance deteriorates (Fig 1.40).
Figure 1.40 The effect of random, casual resistance training over the long term
The gains in strength are rapid during the first few months, a period of several months of fairly stable performance 
follows, until stagnation ensues, especially if there is unskilled use of progressive loading and inadequate training 
variety. Finally, the individual becomes unable to maintain sufficient motivation and central nervous stimulation 
to make further progress. This entire process of adaptation or failure to adapt to physical training has been 
explained by two theoretical models:
• Single-Factor Model of Training (The Supercompensation Model)
• Two-Factor Model of Training (The Fitncss-Fatigue Model)

The single-factor model may be better understood in the light of Selye's GAS model, which provides a theoretical 
foundation for the principle of supercompensation  (Fig 1.41), whereby bodily processes are hypothesised to

optimal if it is imposed when supercompensation has peaked (at point B); this enables the load to be increased 
regularly without causing stagnation or overloading (Fig 1.

The Two-Factor Model  (or Fitness-Fatigue Model) of the training process involves the superimposition of two

shorter-lasting negative factor that decreases preparedness (Fig 1.42).
The fatigue effect, though relatively short in duration, displays a greater magnitude than the fitness effect

preparedness, AP, produced by the summation of the fitness and fatigue after-effects (Fig 1.42). Research has 
described the fitness-fatigue relationship in terms of equations such as the following (Banister et al, 1992):
Preparedness at a time t = Initial Preparedness + Change in Preparedness due to one workout

# The 3:1 Fatigue-to-Fitness Ratio

**What it is** — Zatsiorsky and Kraemer (cited by Bompa) propose that the fatigue from a training bout dissipates roughly **three times faster** than the positive training effect persists — e.g., fatigue lasts ~24 hr while the fitness benefit lasts ~72 hr. The positive effect only becomes *visible* once the masking fatigue has cleared; adaptation and improved performance surface afterward.

**Why it works** — A session produces two aftereffects with different time courses: a large but short-lived fatigue, and a smaller but longer-lasting fitness gain. Early after the bout, fatigue dominates and hides the gain (the "delayed training effect"); as fatigue decays faster, the net effect turns positive. This is the practical core of the fitness–fatigue (two-factor) model.

**When to apply** — Estimating when a quality will "show up" after hard work; spacing testing or competition far enough past a heavy session that fatigue has cleared; explaining why athletes feel worse before they feel better.

**When NOT to apply** — The 3:1 figure is a rule of thumb, not a constant. Training type shifts it — anaerobic work is more fatiguing and lengthens the ratio; CNS-intensive work can extend fatigue well past 24 hr. Don't use it to schedule to the hour. Pairs with [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]] and [[framework--three-training-effects]].

**Example** — Avoiding a max-strength test in the 24 hr after a heavy, novel eccentric session — waiting ~72 hr so the strength gain is no longer masked by residual fatigue and DOMS.

in swimming in terms of a unit of training termed the Training Impulse  (TRIMP). They used the Training Impulse

Zatsiorsky (1995) has stated that, with respect to one training session of average intensity, the fitness effect 
endures roughly three times longer than the fatigue effect (i.e. T1= 3.T2). Thus, if the last negative traces of 
fatigue of a given workout have faded after 2 days, then the positive fitness traces will persist for about 6 days. 
In applying such a model, it is relevant to note that different muscle groups recover at different rates 
(heterochronically) and that the characteristics of the fatigue process may be modified by other adjunct training or 
restoration. Some Russian restoration specialists, therefore, advocate that restorative procedures (such as 
massage) should not always be used on all muscle groups after each session or in the same sequence, because 
supercompensation tends to be more pronounced on a basis of partial restoration (see Ch 8).
More recently* a considerable amount of research has examined the relationship between fitness and fatigue 
and has produced a variety of systems models to enable the training process to be devised more accurately, 
especially with regard to the tapering process  before competitions (Busso et al, 1994; Mujika et al, 1996; Busso 
etal, 1990; Houmard 1991)
Some of this work has suggested that presently accepted forms of tapering for competition may remain too 
rigorous and short to achieve the best result possible from the training undertaken (Fitz-Clarke et al, 1991). These 
results demonstrate that proper placement of training volume during taper is a key factor in optimising 
performance for a specific competition, with a high volume of training in the immediate days preceding an event 
possibly being detrimental to optimal performance (Zarkadas et al, 1995; Mujika et al, 1996; Shepley et al, 1992).
The Concept of Progressive Overload Training
The concept of progressive overloading is proliferated probably more vigorously than any other principle in 
fitness training. This ancient principle states that strength and all other components of fitness increase if the 
training gradually becomes more demanding.
It was known to the legendary Grecian-Italian hero, Milo, who at an early age began lifting a newly-bom bull. 
As the b

grown beast. This, according to legend, is why Milo became so powerful. Today, essentially the same training 
principle, now known as gradual overload or progressive gradual overload, is followed by most serious athletes.
This story or its underlying principle appears in numerous textbooks, without much critical analysis, despite 
the fact that the methodology of periodisation actually contradicts this principle in important respects. The 
major limitation of the gradual overload principle is obvious, namely that a stagnation point is reached, despite 
further increase in loading. The performance growth curve flattens out and a limit to further growth is reached 
This phenomenon is what prevents the same person from constandy breaking world records.
Closer examination of the Milo tale reveals an incomplete ending. Milo, being an enterprising strongman, 
obviously would have sought further strength increase by lifting progressively heavier bulls. If he had progressed 
very gradually, the implications are that he should have been lifting well over 500kg after a few years. Similarly,

week, you should be lifting 580kg at the age of 26 and 1100kg at the age of 36 years. That this will not happen ii 
obvious. In other words, progressive overloading produces diminishing, and ultimately zero, returns.
Research and clinical records also reveal that more intensive loading produces an increase in injury rate well 
before one's physical limits are reached. This is why Russian research produced periodisation models which 
involve phases of decreased loading, so that the curve of training intensity fluctuates upwards and downwards in

with tissue stress and breakdown, whereas decreases in loading promote repair and restoration.

monotonic increases in loading do not occur for any prolonged period. The expression monotonic increase,

1.16.4 A Model of Physical Fitness
The definition of fitness given earlier needs to be expanded to incorporate all the essential factors which 
contribute to this state. Fitness comprises a series of interrelated structural and functional factors which 
conveniently may be referred to as the basic S-factors of fitness: Strength, Speed, Stamina  (general systemic en­
durance or local muscular endurance). Suppleness  (flexibility), Skill  (neuromuscular efficiency), Structure  
(somatotype, size, shape) and Spirit (psychological preparedness). Within the scope of skill, there is also a 
fitness quality known as Style, the individual manner of expressing a particular skill.
Unlike work capacity (1.5), fitness is described not simply by laboratory measurements of qualities such as 
cardiovascular function, muscle strength and flexibility, but also by the specificity of fitness required for each 
activity or sport, which depends to a major extent on neuromotor skills. It is the primary purpose of this book 
to concentrate on the specificity associated with all of the fitness factors related to strength, to analyse how these 
factors interact to provide a form of fitness which is fairly specific to each sport, and to show the reader how to 
devise appropriate models for designing strength training programmes for a given sport.
A comprehensive model of physical fitness may be constructed from the functional motor elements of 
fitness, as shown in Figure 1.45. The model may be developed in two stages: firstly, as a triangular model which 
interrelates strength, stamina (muscular endurance), speed and suppleness (flexibility), and secondly, as a more 
complete pyramidal model which interrelates all of these factors with the process which makes all movement 
possible, namely neuromuscular control  or skill.

speed, which changes along a continuum from the static (speed = 0) to the dynamic state. However, this 
convenient picture could be complicated by including the quasi-isometric state which can influence production of

# Progressive Overload and the Threshold of Adaptation

**What it is** — Adaptation follows a load-dependent sequence with three outcomes: increasing, varied stimulus ⇒ adaptation ⇒ performance improvement; a *standard* (unchanging) load ⇒ plateau ⇒ stagnation; an *excessive* load ⇒ maladaptation ⇒ decline (overreaching/overtraining). Improvement requires systematically crossing the current "threshold of adaptation" by raising intensity, volume, or frequency — then doing so again once the body has adapted.

**Why it works** — Training is beneficial only insofar as it overloads the system enough to demand adaptation. A stimulus below threshold provokes no change; a sustained intolerable stimulus injures or overtrains. Bompa stresses that overload must be paired with **variation** to keep maximizing adaptation rather than habituating.

**When to apply** — The default logic for advancing any program; diagnosing a plateau ("is the load still progressing, or has it gone standard?"); justifying planned increases over a block.

**When NOT to apply** — Not a license for linear, monotonic load increase indefinitely — that path leads to the maladaptation branch. The *rate* and *form* of progression must respect recovery and training age. Overload without adequate recovery is how you cross into overreaching. Pairs with [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]] (recovery side) and is bounded by [[heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]].

**Example** — A strength block uses loads >80% 1RM and nudges intensity/volume upward each microcycle; when testing shows a plateau, the coach changes the stimulus (exercise, tempo, rep scheme) rather than simply repeating the same successful load.

# "Adaptive Reconstruction" vs. "Supercompensation": Verkhoshansky/Siff's Sharper Critique

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (via Siff) argues "adaptive reconstruction" is a more
accurate term than "supercompensation" for the body's response to training load, for two
specific reasons stated in the text: (1) enhanced performance is not simply the result of
increased stores of bioenergetic substances (the energy-overshoot picture supercompensation
implies), but also of structural changes in muscle and connective tissue and enhanced
efficiency of bioenergetic and neuromuscular processing; (2) no supercompensation has been
observed for any bioenergetic substance except glycogen — other biochemicals deplete under
strenuous exercise but do not overshoot their baseline afterward, and each returns to
baseline on its own timeline, making the timing of a "supercompensation window" for
non-glycogen substances indeterminate. Russian sources use "Current Adaptation Reserves"
(CAR) for the readily-available (superficial) and emergency (deep) energy sources drawn on
during Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome resistance phase. (PDF pp. 94-96, printed pp.
83-85.)

**Why it works** — If supercompensation literally meant every adaptation-relevant substance
or structure overshoots baseline on a predictable clock, timing the next training stimulus
to "catch the peak" would be a precise science; the empirical finding that this overshoot
pattern is essentially unique to glycogen undercuts that precision and supports treating
"the next stimulus should land on a rebound" as a general heuristic, not a substance-by-
substance timing rule.

**When to apply** — This library already carries the supercompensation model in
[[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]], which itself notes
"contemporary sport science largely prefers the fitness-fatigue (two-factor) model over
literal supercompensation" and recommends treating supercompensation "as a useful mental
model, not a measured prescription." **Inference:** this entry adds the specific mechanism
for that caution (structural/efficiency changes beyond energy stores, and the
glycogen-only overshoot finding) and the CAR terminology, which the Bompa entry does not
include; use both together rather than duplicating either.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` because it is itself a critique of
a still widely-taught model (supercompensation), argued from a mix of established fact
(structural adaptation beyond energy stores) and an absence-of-evidence claim (no
overshoot observed for other biochemicals) that could be revised by newer measurement
techniques. **Inference:** don't treat "adaptive reconstruction" as a rejection of
periodization practice built on supercompensation timing; the text itself notes
supercompensation theory, despite its shortcomings, had a profound and still-useful impact
on periodization design.

**Example** — **Inference:** glycogen loading before an endurance event is a legitimate
application of true supercompensation; assuming a similarly precise "peak window" exists
for, say, connective tissue remodeling or neuromuscular efficiency gains is not supported
by the same evidence.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] (reciprocal link
recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.16 sharpens the "useful mental model, not a
measured prescription" caution with the specific glycogen-only-overshoot finding and the
CAR/adaptive-reconstruction terminology).

# Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops

**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), Verkhoshansky states biochemical adaptation to
training follows a definite sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first, oxidative ATP
resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle protein (myosin)
and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase; only after that
does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining or detraining, these
adaptations are lost in the reverse order they were gained. The longer the training period,
the more thorough the adaptation and the longer those biochemical changes persist after
training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels). This gain/loss asymmetry across
different systems is termed heterochronic (different tissues and processes change on
different timelines). Overtraining specifically shows a distinct pattern: reduced
glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/glycogen, blood plasma
dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to disrupted acid-base
balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed pp. 85-86.)

**Why it works** — Different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity, structural protein
synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular mechanisms with
different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts, then de-adapts"
model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while others are gained
late and lost early.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's own conditioning material states
that traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining, while traits
hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest, and uses this ordering to sequence how
often each quality needs re-exposure (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md p.47`). **Inference:** this converges directionally with
Platonov's heterochronic principle (different systems have different adaptation/de-
adaptation timelines) but the two are not a stated one-to-one match — the baseline's
build-easy/lose-fast claim is about energy-system categories (aerobic vs. alactic), while
Platonov's sequence is about biochemical sub-processes within training generally (oxidative
capacity, structural protein, glycolysis, CP). Treat them as parallel instances of the same
underlying heterochronicity concept, not as the same specific claim restated.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific ordering (oxidative/glycogen, then
structural protein/glycolysis, then CP) is cited to one secondary source (Platonov, 1988)
without the underlying primary data described in this text; do not treat this exact
four-stage sequence as a settled, universally-timed protocol for monitoring detraining. Use
it as a general principle (adaptation and loss are not uniform across systems) rather than
a specific testing checklist.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete returning from a multi-week layoff might show
CP-system/power qualities holding up relatively better than the earlier-gained oxidative
and glycogen-storage qualities, or vice versa, depending on the specific loss sequence;
either way, "detraining" is not a single uniform decline and re-testing across qualities
(not just one) gives a more accurate readiness picture.

**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].

# The Two-Factor Model Can Be Formalized Mathematically, and Its Research Base Argues Against Heavy Training Right Before Competition

**What it is** — The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Model treats preparedness at time t as
initial preparedness plus the summed effect of a slow-decaying fitness after-effect and a
faster-decaying fatigue after-effect, each with its own magnitude and decay-time constant
(Banister et al., 1992). Banister and Calvert (1980) originated this with the Training
Impulse (TRIMP), a quantified unit of training load used to model and predict elite
swimming performance from the fitness/fatigue balance. Zatsiorsky (1995) is cited for the
same 3:1 fitness-to-fatigue decay ratio already in this library's Bompa material. Later
research building on this model examined tapering specifically: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991)
found presently accepted taper protocols may be too rigorous and short for best results,
and several studies (Zarkadas et al. 1995; Mujika et al. 1996; Shepley et al. 1992) found
that proper placement of training volume during a taper is a key optimization factor, with
high training volume in the days immediately preceding competition possibly detrimental to
performance. Different muscle groups recover heterochronically, which is why some Russian
restoration specialists deliberately avoid applying restorative methods (e.g. massage) to
every muscle group after every session, since supercompensation is reportedly more
pronounced with partial rather than total restoration. (PDF pp. 99-100, printed pp. 88-89.)

**Why it works** — Modeling preparedness as the sum of two exponentially-decaying
after-effects with different time constants gives periodization a quantitative structure
(not just a qualitative "wave" description), which is what allows taper researchers to ask
a specific, testable question: how much and how recently loaded should training be before
competition to maximize the fitness-minus-fatigue difference at competition time.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the more technical, equation-based underpinning
of this library's already-captured practical rule
([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]); cite this entry when a
more rigorous or quantitative framing is needed (e.g. explaining the model to a sport
scientist or in a research-facing document), and cite the Bompa heuristic for the everyday
coaching rule of thumb. The taper-volume finding directly supports reducing training
volume, not just intensity, in the days immediately before a competition or key testing
date.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific mathematical constants (A, B, T1, T2)
must be fit per individual and per training phase, and the text notes they require
periodic re-estimation; do not treat this as a plug-and-play formula without that
fitting process. The taper studies cited are from the early-to-mid 1990s and largely from
swimming; **Inference:** don't assume the exact taper-volume findings transfer unchanged to
football or other team sports without independent verification.

**Example** — **Inference:** rather than assuming a flat "taper week" cuts intensity but
keeps volume similar, this model's logic and the cited taper research both point toward
deliberately reducing volume (not just easing intensity) in the final days before a key
competition or test date, to let the longer-lasting fitness effect show through as the
shorter fatigue effect clears.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]],
[[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].

# The S-Factors Pyramidal Model of Fitness (Strength, Speed, Stamina, Suppleness, Skill, Structure, Spirit)

**What it is** — A comprehensive model of fitness built from seven "S-factors": Strength,
Speed, Stamina (systemic or local muscular endurance), Suppleness (flexibility), Skill
(neuromuscular efficiency, including a "Style" sub-quality — an individual's manner of
expressing a skill), Structure (somatotype, size, shape), and Spirit (psychological
preparedness). The model is built in two stages: a triangular base relating strength,
stamina, speed, and suppleness, then a pyramid adding skill/neuromuscular control as the
process that makes all movement possible, with flexibility placed at the center of the
base because range of movement underlies expression of every other quality. From the
pairwise relationships between factors, an extended list of compound fitness qualities is
derived: static/dynamic strength and strength-endurance, strength-speed, speed-strength,
strength-speed endurance, speed, endurance, flexibility-strength, flexibility-endurance,
flexibility-speed, skill, strength-skill, flexibility-skill, speed-skill, and
skill-endurance. Relative versions of these qualities (per unit bodymass) matter
separately in sports where bodymass is constrained (e.g. weight-class sports). (PDF pp.
102-103, printed pp. 91-92.)

**Why it works** — Rather than treating strength, speed, endurance, and flexibility as
four independent boxes, this model treats them as vertices whose pairwise and triple
combinations describe most of the specific fitness qualities that actually appear in
sport (e.g. "speed-strength" and "strength-speed" as two distinct qualities depending on
which end of the force-velocity spectrum dominates, already discussed in
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]), with skill/
neuromuscular control cutting across all of them.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful as a master vocabulary/reference when precisely
naming which quality a given test or exercise targets (e.g. distinguishing
"strength-speed" training from "speed-strength" training, or "flexibility-strength" from
plain flexibility), and as a teaching framework (e.g. HHPR 5355) for showing students why
"fitness" is not one thing to test or train, but a structured set of specific,
combinable qualities.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky himself calls this model "representational or
descriptive rather than scientifically analytical" and notes it is complicated by other
factors such as quasi-isometric states at very slow speeds (PDF p. 102, printed p. 91);
**Inference:** don't treat it as a validated measurement taxonomy with defined tests for
each named compound quality — most of these terms (e.g. "flexibility-skill") have no
standard test attached in this text.

**Example** — **Inference:** describing an athlete's need as "relative strength-speed"
(power per unit bodymass) rather than just "power" gives a program design target that is
precise about both the force-velocity region and the bodymass constraint, useful for a
weight-class or position-limited athlete.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]],
[[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]].

# The S-Factors Pyramidal Model of Fitness (Strength, Speed, Stamina, Suppleness, Skill, Structure, Spirit)

**What it is** — A comprehensive model of fitness built from seven "S-factors": Strength,
Speed, Stamina (systemic or local muscular endurance), Suppleness (flexibility), Skill
(neuromuscular efficiency, including a "Style" sub-quality — an individual's manner of
expressing a skill), Structure (somatotype, size, shape), and Spirit (psychological
preparedness). The model is built in two stages: a triangular base relating strength,
stamina, speed, and suppleness, then a pyramid adding skill/neuromuscular control as the
process that makes all movement possible, with flexibility placed at the center of the
base because range of movement underlies expression of every other quality. From the
pairwise relationships between factors, an extended list of compound fitness qualities is
derived: static/dynamic strength and strength-endurance, strength-speed, speed-strength,
strength-speed endurance, speed, endurance, flexibility-strength, flexibility-endurance,
flexibility-speed, skill, strength-skill, flexibility-skill, speed-skill, and
skill-endurance. Relative versions of these qualities (per unit bodymass) matter
separately in sports where bodymass is constrained (e.g. weight-class sports). (PDF pp.
102-103, printed pp. 91-92.)

**Why it works** — Rather than treating strength, speed, endurance, and flexibility as
four independent boxes, this model treats them as vertices whose pairwise and triple
combinations describe most of the specific fitness qualities that actually appear in
sport (e.g. "speed-strength" and "strength-speed" as two distinct qualities depending on
which end of the force-velocity spectrum dominates, already discussed in
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]), with skill/
neuromuscular control cutting across all of them.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful as a master vocabulary/reference when precisely

"strength-speed" training from "speed-strength" training, or "flexibility-strength" from
plain flexibility), and as a teaching framework (e.g. HHPR 5355) for showing students why
"fitness" is not one thing to test or train, but a structured set of specific,
combinable qualities.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky himself calls this model "representational or
descriptive rather than scientifically analytical" and notes it is complicated by other
factors such as quasi-isometric states at very slow speeds (PDF p. 102, printed p. 91);
**Inference:** don't treat it as a validated measurement taxonomy with defined tests for
each named compound quality — most of these terms (e.g. "flexibility-skill") have no
standard test attached in this text.

(power per unit bodymass) rather than just "power" gives a program design target that is
